### 5.2 Proof of Theorem 1.3

We begin by proving the stated claims about the communication, time, and space complexities, and then proceed to prove correctness.

#### 5.2.1 Algorithmic Complexity

We’ve already shown by Definition 5.1 that the length of the encoding $\mathsf{enc}(x)$ is $m=O_{\varepsilon}(n^{2+4\delta})$ . We begin by proving the computational complexity claim.

#### Lemma 5.2.

If $A$ runs in time $t$ , Algorithm 2 runs in time $m\cdot O_{\varepsilon,\delta}\left(1+\frac{t}{n^{2}}\right)$ .

#### Proof.

Notice that each function $g_{i}(x_{i})$ is computed exactly $\frac{\log^{2}n\cdot M_{n}}{n}$ times throughout the protocol. (To see this, one can show inductively that $\frac{1}{j-i}$ fraction of the $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ ’s in the computation of $A(i,j)$ are used towards the decoding of each $x_{k}$ , $k\in(i,j]$ .) Other than that, one must decode of each of the $\log^{2}n\cdot M_{n}$ copies of $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ throughout the stream, each of which takes $N(n)+\text{polylog}(n)$ time to read and decode (see Theorem 4.1). This gives a total computation time of $\log^{2}n\cdot M(n)\cdot\left(N(n)+\text{polylog}(r)+\frac{t}{n}\right)=O_{\varepsilon,\delta}\left(m\cdot\left(1+\frac{t}{n^{2}}\right)\right)$ . ∎

Next, we show that Algorithm 1 satisfies the required space guarantees. We’ll first show that the confidences $c$ can be stored in $O_{\delta}(\log n)$ bits.

#### Lemma 5.3.

For any $i,j,q$ where $j-i$ is a power of $r$ , let $(\hat{q},\hat{c}):=\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ . It holds that $\hat{c}$ can be computed and stored as a fraction $(c_{1},c_{2})=c_{1}/c_{2}$ where $c_{1}\leq c_{2}=(j-i)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q$ .

#### Proof.

We show this by induction on $j-i$ for $j-i\leq n$ . For the base case where $j-i=1$ , this statement holds by Theorem 4.1 since $c_{2}=4Q$ .

Assume the statement holds for all $q^{\prime}$ and $j^{\prime}-i^{\prime}<j-i$ where $j^{\prime}-i^{\prime}$ is a power of $r$ . In the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ , for $a\in r$ , each value of $c_{a}$ is ultimately the sum of $\leq\ell$ values outputted by the function $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a})$ . Since $\frac{i_{a}-i_{a-1}}{r}=\frac{j-i}{r}$ , we can use the induction hypothesis to write each value as a fraction with denominator $\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q$ . Then, each $c_{a}/\ell$ is a fraction with denominator

$$ \left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q\cdot\ell=\ell^{\log_{r}\frac{j-i}{r}}\cdot 4Q\cdot\ell=\ell^{\log_{r}(j-i)}\cdot 4Q=(j-i)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q, $$

and so the output confidence $\min_{a\in[r]}\{c_{a}/\ell\}$ can be written with denominator $c_{2}=(j-i)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q$ . ∎

Now, we return to showing that Algorithm 1 satisfies the required space guarantees.

#### Lemma 5.4.

Algorithm 1 uses $s\cdot O_{\varepsilon}\left((\log n)^{O(1/\delta)}\right)$ bits of space.

#### Proof.

Define $\alpha=\alpha(n)=O_{\varepsilon}(\log^{O(1/\delta)}n)$ to be the runtime and thus an upper bound on the space required in the local decoding with confidence of $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ as given in Theorem 4.1. We claim the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(0,n)$ takes $\alpha+s+\log_{r}n\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right)$ bits of storage. We show by induction on $j-i$ (where $j-i$ is a power of $r$ that the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ requires at most $\alpha+s+\log_{r}(j-i)\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right)$ bits of space.

The base case holds because when $j-i=1$ because then only $\alpha+s$ space is required.

For the inductive step, the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ requires $\ell$ computations of $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a})$ for each $a\in[r]$ . By the inductive hypothesis, each such computation takes $\alpha+s+\log_{r}\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right)$ bits of space. Each such computation is done in series, and between iterations only the pairs $\{(q_{a},c_{a})\}_{a\in[r]}$ are tracked. Each $q_{a}$ is a state of size $s$ . Each $c_{a}$ is the sum of $\leq\ell$ confidences that are the output of computation $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a})$ . By Lemma 6.3 the output confidence of $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a})$ is a fraction $\leq 1$ with denominator $\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q$ , so $c_{a}$ can be represented in $2\log_{2}\left(\ell\cdot\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q\right)<O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log_{2}n)$ bits. Moreover, in each chunk, we must compute a permutation of $r$ , which takes at most $r\log_{2}r=r\cdot o_{\delta}(\log n)$ bits. In total, this takes

$$ \displaystyle\leq\left[\alpha+s+\log_{r}\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right)\right]+r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right) \displaystyle=\alpha+s+\log_{r}\left(j-i\right)\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right) $$

bits of space, as desired.

Finally, the amplification part of Algorithm 2 requires $\log^{2}n$ iterations. Between iterations, we are only storing a pair $(q,c)$ . This increases the number of bits required by at most $s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)$ .

In total, the total space needed throughout the entire algorithm is

$$ <s\cdot\log^{1/\delta+1}n+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log^{1/\delta+2}n)+\alpha<s\cdot O_{\varepsilon}\left((\log n)^{O(1/\delta)}\right) $$

bits. ∎

#### 5.2.2 Correctness

We now show correctness. Formally, correctness is shown by the following lemma.

#### Lemma 5.5.

When at most $\frac{1}{4}-\varepsilon$ fraction of the stream $\mathsf{enc}(x)$ is corrupted, Algorithm 1 outputs $A(x)$ with probability $\geq 1-\exp{(-\varepsilon^{2}\log^{2}n/32)}$ .

We prove the following statement which will easily imply Lemma 5.5. For a given $i,j$ and associated string that is read by the algorithm in the computation, let the random variable $(q(i,j),c(i,j))$ denote the state and confidence after the computation $\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ . We define the signed confidence, denoted $c^{\pm}(i,j)$ , to be defined as $+c(i,j)$ if $q(i,j)=A_{i,j}(x)$ and $-c(i,j)$ otherwise. For intuition, the more positive $c^{\pm}(i,j)$ is, the more correct with higher confidence the output $(q(i,j),c(i,j))$ is, whereas the more negative $c_{\pm}(i,j)$ is, the more $q(i,j)$ is incorrect with high confidence. So, $c^{\pm}(i,j)$ gives us a scaled measure of how correct the output of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ is.

#### Lemma 5.6.

For any $0\leq i<j\leq n$ and $e\in\mathbb{R}$ , given $\leq\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log(j-i)}{\log n}-e$ fraction of corruptions in the bits read by the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ , we have $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j)]>e$ .

We defer the proof to Section 5.2.3 and return to the proof of Lemma 5.5.

#### Proof of Lemma 5.5.

In the special case where $i=0,j=n$ and there are $\leq\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}-e<\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log(j-i)}{r}-e$ errors (where the inequality follows because $\log n<\varepsilon\cdot r$ ), by Lemma 5.6 we have that $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(0,n)]>e$ .

Then, the final amplification step of the protocol computes the pair $(q(0,n),c(0,n))$ for $\log^{2}n$ times, where in each chunk $i$ we denote the fraction of error to be $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}-e_{i}\right)$ , where $\sum_{i}e_{i}\geq\frac{\varepsilon\log^{2}n}{2}$ since we assumed the total error was $\leq\frac{1}{4}-\varepsilon$ . Also, the protocol outputs $A(x)$ if and only if $\sum_{i}c^{\pm}_{i}(0,n)$ (denoting the value of $c^{\pm}(0,n)$ in the $i$ ’th chunk) is positive. By Azuma’s inequality,

$$ Pr\left[\sum_{i}c^{\pm}_{i}(0,n)>0\right]\geq Pr\left[\sum_{i}\left(c^{\pm}_{i}(0,n)-e_{i}\right)>-\frac{\varepsilon\log^{2}n}{2}\right]\geq 1-\exp\left(-\frac{\varepsilon^{2}\log^{2}n}{32}\right). $$

∎

Combining Lemmas 5.2, 5.4, and 5.5, this concludes the proof of Theorem 1.3.

#### 5.2.3 Proof of Lemma 5.6

We prove Lemma 5.6 by induction on $j-i$ . We’ll show the statement assuming it holds for $j^{\prime}-i^{\prime}<j-i$ (where $j^{\prime}-i^{\prime}$ is a power of $r$ ).

We begin with the base case of $j-i=1$ . In this case, the algorithm simply reads (a corrupted version of) $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ , and by Theorem 4.1, it holds that $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j)]>e$ since there is at most $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-e\right)$ error.

We start with some useful notation. In the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ , we say that the output of the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a})$ in the $b$ ’th chunk is $(\hat{q}_{a,b},\hat{c}_{a,b})$ . We define the signed confidence $\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}$ to be the confidence $\hat{c}_{a,b}$ signed by whether the guess $\hat{q}_{a,b}$ is correct: that is,

$$ \hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}:=\begin{cases}\hat{c}_{a,b}&\text{$\hat{q}_{a,b}=A_{i_{a-1},i_{a}}(x)$}\\
-\hat{c}_{a,b}&\text{$\hat{q}_{a,b}\neq A_{i_{a-1},i_{a}}(x)$}.\end{cases} $$

The cumulative best guess and confidence for $A_{i_{a-1},i_{a}}(x)$ after all $\ell$ chunks is denoted by $(q_{a},c_{a})$ . We let $q_{0}=\emptyset$ . We define a cumulative signed confidence $c^{\pm}_{a}$ as follows:

$$ c^{\pm}_{a}:=\begin{cases}c_{a}&\text{$q_{a}=A_{i_{a-1},i_{a}}(x)$}\\
-c_{a}&\text{$q_{a}\neq A_{i_{a-1},i_{a}}(x)$}.\end{cases} $$

We show a lower bound on the cumulative signed confidence at the end of all $\ell$ chunks $c^{\pm}_{a}$ that holds with high probability.

#### Lemma 5.7.

Let $a\in[r]$ index the $r$ intervals $(i_{a-1},i_{a}]$ in the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ . Let each of the $\ell$ chunks in the computation be indexed by $b\in[\ell]$ and suppose chunk $b$ has $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{j-i}{r}}{\log n}-e_{b}\right)$ fraction of corruption. Then, for all $a\in[r]$ , with probability $\geq 1-\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{8}\right)$ it holds that $c^{\pm}_{a}>\sum_{b\leq\ell}e_{b}-\frac{\ell}{\log n}$ .

#### Proof.

We first show that for all $a$ , it holds that $c^{\pm}_{a}\geq\sum_{b\leq\ell}\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}$ . To see this, define $c^{\pm}_{a,b}$ to be the value of $c_{a}$ at the end of chunk $b$ if $q_{a}$ is correct at the end of chunk $b$ , and otherwise, $-c_{a}$ , so that $c^{\pm}_{a}=c^{\pm}_{a,\ell}$ . Then, $c^{\pm}_{a,b}-c^{\pm}_{a,b-1}\geq\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}$ , which implies that $c^{\pm}_{a}\geq\sum_{b\leq\ell}\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}$ .

Consider the sequence $\left\{X_{b}:=\sum_{d\leq b}\left(\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,d}-e_{d}\right)\right\}_{b\in[\ell]}$ . Because $\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}\right]>e_{b}$ by induction on induction on $j-i$ , the sequence $\{X_{b}\}_{b\in[\ell]}$ is a submartingale. It also holds that $|\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}-e_{b}|\leq 2$ .

Then, by Azuma’s inequality, it holds that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr\left[c^{\pm}_{a}>\sum_{b\leq\ell}e_{b}-\frac{\ell}{\log n}\right]\geq Pr\left[X_{\ell}>-\frac{\ell}{\log n}\right]>1-\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{8}\right). $$

∎

Now, we need a way to reconcile the values of $e$ and $e_{b}$ . Recall that from the statement of Lemma 5.6 that $e$ is defined to be such that there is $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log{j-i}}{\log n}-e\right)$ fraction of error in the bits read by $\mathsf{estA}(i,j)$ . In Lemma 5.7, chunk $b$ had $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{j-i}{r}}{\log n}-e_{b}\right)$ fraction of error. This means that the total fraction of error is equal to

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log(j-i)}{\log n}-e \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\ell}\sum_{b\leq\ell}\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{j-i}{r}}{\log n}-e_{b}\right) \displaystyle\implies e \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\ell}\cdot\sum_{b\leq\ell}e_{b}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log r}{\log n}. $$

Next, we show that the cumulative signed confidence is larger than proportional to $e$ at the end of each of the $\ell$ chunks.

#### Lemma 5.8.

With probability at least $1-\frac{1}{n}$ , it holds that for all $a\in[r]$ that $\frac{c^{\pm}_{a}}{\ell}>e+\frac{1}{\log n}$ .

#### Proof.

Using Lemma 5.7 with a union bound, it holds with probability at least

$$ \displaystyle 1-\sum_{1\leq a\leq r}\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{8}\right)\geq 1-r\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{8}\right)\geq 1-\frac{1}{n} $$

that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{c^{\pm}_{a}}{\ell} \displaystyle>\frac{\sum_{b\leq\ell}e_{b}-\frac{\ell}{\log n}}{\ell}\geq e+\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log r}{\log n}-\frac{1}{\log n}\geq e+\frac{1}{\log n} $$

since for sufficiently large $n$ it holds that $\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\log r>2$ . ∎

We return to the computation of $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j)]$ . Note that

$$ c^{\pm}(i,j)=\begin{cases}+\min_{a\in[r]}\{\frac{c_{a}}{\ell}\}&q(i,j)=A_{i,j}(x)\\
-\min_{a\in[r]}\{\frac{c_{a}}{\ell}\}&q(i,j)\neq A_{i,j}(x).\end{cases} $$

Define the event $E$ to be the event where $\frac{c^{\pm}_{a}}{\ell}>e+\frac{1}{\log n}$ for all $a\in[r]$ . By Lemma 5.8, $E$ holds with probability at least $1-\frac{1}{n}$ . We split the proof of Lemma 5.6 based on whether $e+\frac{1}{\log n}\geq 0$ .

If $e+\frac{1}{\log n}\geq 0$ , then whenever $E$ holds we have that for all $a$ we have $c^{\pm}_{a}>0$ and thus $q(i,j)=A_{i,j}(x)$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j)] \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\min_{a\in[r]}\left\{\frac{c_{a}}{\ell}\right\}\Bigg|E\right]\cdot\Pr[E]+(\text{min value of $c^{\pm}(i,j)$})\cdot\left(1-\Pr[E]\right) \displaystyle>\left(e+\frac{1}{\log n}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)+(-1)\cdot\frac{1}{n} \displaystyle=e+\frac{n-e\log{n}-1-\log n}{n\log n} \displaystyle>e. $$

If $e+\frac{1}{\log n}<0$ , then if $q(i,j)=A_{i,j}(x)$ , then $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j)]\geq 0>e+\frac{1}{\log n}\geq e$ . Otherwise, there is at least one value of $a$ for which $q_{a}$ is incorrect. Conditioned on $E$ , it holds that $\frac{c^{\pm}_{a}}{\ell}>e+\frac{1}{\log n}$ . Since $q_{a}$ is incorrect it holds that $c^{\pm}_{a}=-c_{a}$ , implying that $\frac{c_{a}}{\ell}<-e-\frac{1}{\log n}$ . As such,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j)] \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\left[-\min_{a\in[r]}\left\{\frac{c_{a}}{\ell}\right\}\Bigg|E\right]\cdot\Pr[E]+(\text{min value of $c^{\pm}(i,j)$})\cdot\left(1-\Pr[E]\right) \displaystyle>\left(e+\frac{1}{\log n}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)+(-1)\cdot\frac{1}{n} \displaystyle=e+\frac{n-e\log{n}-1-\log n}{n\log n} \displaystyle>e. $$

This concludes the proof of Lemma 5.6.

## 6 Noise Resilient Streaming for General Algorithms

We now consider general streaming algorithms, whose computational may be sequential in nature. Our main result is a noise resilient conversion for deterministic streaming algorithms $A$ . Compared to our scheme for linear algorithms from Section 5, the length of our encoding is larger: $n^{4+\delta}$ compared to $n^{2+\delta}$ .

See 1.1

Throughout this section, we use the notation

$$ A(q,\hat{x})\in\{0,1\}^{s} $$

to denote the state of algorithm $A$ when starting with the state $q\in\{0,1\}^{s}$ and executing on $\hat{x}$ received in a stream. By definition, there is an explicit algorithm that computes $A(q,\hat{x})$ in $s$ space. We also use the shorthand $A(\hat{x})$ to denote $A(\emptyset,\hat{x})$ . Notice that $A(x)=A(\emptyset,x)$ is simply the output state of the stream.

### 6.1 Statement of Algorithm

Let $\varepsilon>0$ . Throughout the section let $r=\log^{1/\delta}n$ and define $\ell:=r^{2}\log^{4}{n}$ . We also assume for simplicity that $\log_{r}n$ is an integer. We will also assume that $n>\max\left\{\exp(\exp({8\delta/\varepsilon})),\exp(1/\varepsilon)\right\}$ is sufficiently large, so that also $\ell<n$ .

We begin by specifying the encoding $\mathsf{enc}(x)$ that Alice sends in the stream.

#### Definition 6.1 ( $\mathsf{enc}(x)$ ).

Let $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ be a locally decodable code with $N(n)=|\mathsf{LDC}(x)|=O_{\varepsilon}(n^{1+\delta})$ and query complexity $Q=O_{\varepsilon}(\log^{2/\delta}n)$ satisfying the guarantees of Theorem 4.1 for $\varepsilon/8$ . Then Alice sends $\mathsf{enc}(x):=\mathsf{LDC}(x)^{\log^{2}n\cdot M_{n}}$ where $M_{n}=(r\cdot\ell)^{\log_{r}n}$ (that is, $\mathsf{enc}(n)$ is $\log^{2}n\cdot M_{n}$ copies of $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ ). In particular, $m=|\mathsf{enc}(x)|=(r\cdot\ell)^{\log_{r}n}\cdot\log^{2}n\cdot N(n)=O_{\varepsilon}(n^{4+6\delta})$ .

Next, we describe Bob’s streaming algorithm $B_{A}:=B(A)$ . Before stating it formally, we provide a high-level description.

#### Description:

Let $z$ be the incoming stream that Bob receives. At a high level, the algorithm $B_{A}$ runs by generating many guesses for $A(x)$ along with confidences indicating how likely that guess was correct (depending on how much error is witnessed while generating the guess). At the end, the guess that has the most cumulative confidence is outputted.

For $i,j$ where $j-i$ is an integer power of $r$ , we define the algorithm $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ that has the following syntax:

- • $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ takes as input two indices $i,j\in[n]$ along with a state $q\in\{0,1\}^{s}$ which represents a guess for the state of $A(q,x(i:j])$ .

- • It reads $N_{j-i}:=(r\cdot\ell)^{\log_{r}(j-i)}\cdot N(n)$ many bits of $z$ after which it outputs a guess for $A(q,x(i:j])$ along with a confidence.

In particular, $\mathsf{estA}(0,n,q)$ outputs a guess for $A(x)$ along with a confidence. By running $\mathsf{estA}(0,n,q)$ many times and aggregating the guesses weighted by the confidences, we obtain a final output.

At a high level, to compute $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ , we break down the interval $(i:j]$ into $r$ subintervals $(i_{0}:i_{1}],(i_{1}:i_{2}],\dots,(i_{r-1}:i_{r}]$ where $i_{a}=i+a\cdot\frac{j-i}{r}$ . We then recursively formulate guesses for each $A\left(x\left(1:i_{a}\right]\right)$ over many iterations by calling $\mathsf{estA}\left(i_{a-1},i_{a},q_{a-1}\right)$ for some state $q_{a-1}$ . The choice of $a$ in each iteration must be randomized, so that the adversary cannot attack any single choice of $a$ . More specifically, we will split up the $N_{j-i}$ length input stream into $\ell$ chunks, each of length $N_{j-i}/\ell$ bits. Each chunk is split into $r$ sections, each of size $N_{j-i}/(\ell\cdot r)=N_{(j-i)/r}$ . In each chunk, we pick a random permutation $(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\dots,\pi_{r})$ of $[r]$ . In the $a$ ’th section of the chunk, we will compute on the subproblem corresponding to interval $\left(i_{\pi_{a}-1}:i_{\pi_{a}}\right]$ by calling $\mathsf{estA}\left(i_{\pi_{a}-1},i_{\pi_{a}},~q_{\pi_{a}-1}\right)$ .

Note that as the algorithm $A$ is computed sequentially, computing a guess for $A\left(x\left[1:i_{a}\right]\right)$ requires having a starting state $q_{a-1}$ for $A\left(x\left[1:i_{a-1}\right]\right)$ . Thus, throughout the entire computation, we will keep track of the best guess and associated confidence for each of the $r$ states $A\left(x\left[1:i_{a}\right]\right)$ , denoted $(q_{a},c_{a})$ and all initialized to $(\emptyset,0)$ .

These pairs $(q_{a},c_{a})$ are maintained as follows. Whenever a recursive call to $\mathsf{estA}\left(i_{a-1},i_{a},q_{a-1}\right)$ is completed, outputting $(\hat{q},\hat{c})$ , then: if $q_{a}=\hat{q}$ then the confidence $c_{a}$ is increased by $\hat{c}$ , and if $q_{a}\not=\hat{q}$ then the confidence $c_{a}$ is decreased by $\hat{c}$ . If the confidence $c_{a}$ becomes negative, then we are more sure that the correct state is $\hat{q}$ rather than $q_{a}$ : then $q_{a}$ is replaced by $\hat{q}$ and the confidence is negated (so that it’s positive). In this last case where $q_{a}$ is replaced, we have no more reason to believe that further computations of $q_{a^{\prime}}$ , $a^{\prime}>a$ , are correct since they all depended on $q_{a}$ , so we erase all such pairs $(q_{a^{\prime}},c_{a^{\prime}})$ and reset them to $(\emptyset,0)$ . A key point in our analysis is to understand why this does not cause the error probability to accumulate.

*Algorithm 2 Bob’s Noise Resilient Algorithm $B_{A}$*

```
1: input $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and stream $z\in\{0,1\}^{m}$ .
2: function $\mathsf{estA}$ ( $i,j,q$ ) $\triangleright$ compute the state of $A$ starting at state $q$ between steps $i$ and $j$
3: if $j=i+1$ then
4: Read the next $|\mathsf{LDC}(x)|$ bits of the stream $y$ .

6: return $A(q,\hat{b}),c$ .
7: else
8: Let $i_{0}=i,i_{1}=i+\frac{j-i}{r},i_{2}=i+\frac{2(j-i)}{r},\ldots,i_{r}=j$ .
9: Initialize a list of pairs $(q_{1},c_{1}),\ldots(q_{r},c_{r})$ each to $(\emptyset,0)$ . $\triangleright$ cumulative best guesses and confidences
10: for $\ell$ iterations do
11: Let $\pi_{1}\ldots\pi_{r}$ be a random permutation of $[r]$ .
12: Set $(q^{\prime}_{1},c^{\prime}_{1})=(q_{1},c_{1}),\ldots(q^{\prime}_{r},c^{\prime}_{r})=(q_{r},c_{r})$ .
13: for $a\in[r]$ do
14: Compute $(\hat{q},\hat{c})\leftarrow\mathsf{estA}(i_{\pi_{a}-1},i_{\pi_{a}},q^{\prime}_{\pi_{a}-1})$ where $q^{\prime}_{0}:=q$ .

17: else
18: $c_{\pi_{a}}\leftarrow c^{\prime}_{\pi_{a}}-\hat{c}$
19: if $c_{\pi_{a}}<0$ then $\triangleright$ if the guess changes, reset its confidence
20: $q_{\pi_{a}}\leftarrow\hat{q}$ and $c_{\pi_{a}}\leftarrow-c_{\pi_{a}}$ .
21: if some $q_{a}$ was changed from its value at the beginning of the chunk then
22: For all $i>a$ , set $(q_{i},c_{i})\leftarrow(\emptyset,0)$ . $\triangleright$ reset state and confidence for states with $i>a$
23: return $q_{r},\min(c_{1}\ldots c_{r})/\ell$

25: Initialize a pair $(q,c)$ to $(\emptyset,0)$ .
26: for $\log^{2}n$ iterations do $\triangleright$ amplification step
27: Let $(\hat{q},\hat{c})\leftarrow\mathsf{estA}(0,n,\emptyset)$
28: if $\hat{q}=q$ then
29: $c\leftarrow c+\hat{c}$
30: else
31: $c\leftarrow c-\hat{c}$
32: if $c<0$ then
33: $q\leftarrow\hat{q}$ and $c\leftarrow-c$ .
34: output $q$ . $\triangleright$ output $A(x)$
```

### 6.2 Proof of Theorem 1.1

The proofs that the algorithm satisfies the required space, computational and communication guarantees are essentially the same as in Section 5, but we reproduce them for completeness. The proof of correctness is somewhat more complicated but also follows the same general outline.

#### 6.2.1 Algorithmic Complexity

We begin by proving the stated claims about communication, time, and space complexities. We’ve already shown by Definition 6.1 that the length of the encoding $\mathsf{enc}(x)$ is $m=O_{\varepsilon}(n^{4+6\delta})$ . We thus proceed by proving the computational complexity claim.

#### Lemma 6.2.

If $A$ runs in time $t$ , Algorithm 2 runs in time $m\cdot O_{\varepsilon,\delta}\left(1+\frac{t}{n^{2}}\right)$ .

#### Proof.

Notice that each step $A(q_{i-1},x[i])$ is computed exactly $\frac{\log^{2}n\cdot M_{n}}{n}$ times throughout the protocol. (To see this, one can show inductively that $\frac{1}{j-i}$ fraction of the $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ ’s in the computation of $A(i,j,q)$ are used towards the decoding of $x_{k}$ for each $k\in(i,j]$ .) Other than that, one must decode of each of the $\log^{2}n\cdot M_{n}$ copies of $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ throughout the stream, each of which takes $N(n)+\text{polylog}(n)$ time to read and decode (see Theorem 4.1). This gives a total computation time of $\log^{2}n\cdot M(n)\cdot\left(N(n)+\text{polylog}(r)+\frac{t}{n}\right)=O_{\varepsilon,\delta}\left(m\cdot\left(1+\frac{t}{n^{2}}\right)\right)$ . ∎

Next, we show that Algorithm 2 satisfies the required space guarantees. We’ll first show that the confidences $c$ can be stored in $O_{\delta}(\log n)$ bits.

#### Lemma 6.3.

For any $i,j,q$ where $j-i$ is a power of $r$ , let $(\hat{q},\hat{c}):=\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ . It holds that $\hat{c}$ can be computed and stored as a fraction $(c_{1},c_{2})=c_{1}/c_{2}$ where $c_{1}\leq c_{2}=(j-i)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q$ .

#### Proof.

We show this by induction on $j-i$ for $j-i\leq n$ . For the base case where $j-i=1$ , this statement holds by Theorem 4.1 since $c_{2}=4Q$ .

Assume the statement holds for all $q^{\prime}$ and $j^{\prime}-i^{\prime}<j-i$ where $j^{\prime}-i^{\prime}$ is a power of $r$ . In the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ , for $a\in r$ , each value of $c_{a}$ is ultimately the sum of $\leq\ell$ values outputted by the function $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a})$ . Since $\frac{i_{a}-i_{a-1}}{r}=\frac{j-i}{r}$ , we can use the induction hypothesis to write each value as a fraction with denominator $\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q$ . Then, each $c_{a}/\ell$ is a fraction with denominator

$$ \left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q\cdot\ell=\ell^{\log_{r}\frac{j-i}{r}}\cdot 4Q\cdot\ell=\ell^{\log_{r}(j-i)}\cdot 4Q=(j-i)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q, $$

and so the output confidence $\min_{a\in[r]}\{c_{a}/\ell\}$ can be written with denominator $c_{2}=(j-i)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q$ . ∎

Now, we return to showing that Algorithm 2 satisfies the required space guarantees.

#### Lemma 6.4.

Algorithm 2 uses $s\cdot O_{\varepsilon}\left((\log n)^{O(1/\delta)}\right)$ bits of space.

#### Proof.

Define $\alpha=\alpha(n)=O_{\varepsilon}(\log^{O(1/\delta)}n)$ to be the runtime and thus an upper bound on the space required in the local decoding with confidence of $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ as given in Theorem 4.1. We claim the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(0,n,\emptyset)$ takes $\alpha+s+\log_{r}n\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right)$ bits of storage. We show by induction on $j-i$ (where $j-i$ is a power of $r$ that the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ requires at most $\alpha+s+\log_{r}(j-i)\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right)$ bits of space.

The base case holds because when $j-i=1$ because then only $\alpha+s$ space is required.

For the inductive step, the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ requires $\ell$ computations of $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a},q_{a-1})$ for each $a\in[r]$ . By the inductive hypothesis, each such computation takes $\alpha+s+\log_{r}\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right)$ bits of space. Each such computation is done in series, and between iterations only the pairs $\{(q_{a},c_{a})\}_{a\in[r]}$ are tracked. Each $q_{a}$ is a state of size $s$ . Each $c_{a}$ is the sum of $\leq\ell$ confidences that are the output of computation $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a},q_{a-1})$ . By Lemma 6.3 the output confidence of $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a},q_{a-1})$ is a fraction $\leq 1$ with denominator $\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q$ , so $c_{a}$ can be represented in $2\log_{2}\left(\ell\cdot\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)^{\log_{r}\ell}\cdot 4Q\right)<O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log_{2}n)$ bits. Moreover, in each chunk, we must compute a permutation of $r$ , which takes at most $r\log_{2}r=r\cdot o_{\delta}(\log n)$ bits. In total, this takes

$$ \displaystyle\leq\left[\alpha+s+\log_{r}\left(\frac{j-i}{r}\right)\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right)\right]+r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right) \displaystyle=\alpha+s+\log_{r}\left(j-i\right)\cdot r\cdot\left(s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)\right) $$

bits of space, as desired.

Finally, the amplification part of Algorithm 2 requires $\log^{2}n$ iterations. Between iterations, we are only storing a pair $(q,c)$ . This increases the number of bits required by at most $s+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log n)$ .

In total, the total space needed throughout the entire algorithm is

$$ <s\cdot\log^{1/\delta+1}n+O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log^{1/\delta+2}n)+\alpha<s\cdot O_{\varepsilon}\left((\log n)^{O(1/\delta)}\right) $$

bits. ∎

#### 6.2.2 Correctness

Next, we show correctness. Formally, correctness is shown by the following lemma.

#### Lemma 6.5.

When at most $\frac{1}{4}-\varepsilon$ fraction of the stream $\mathsf{enc}(x)$ is corrupted, Algorithm 2 outputs $A(x)$ with probability $\geq 1-\exp{(-\varepsilon^{2}\log^{2}n/32)}$ .

We prove the following statement which will easily imply Lemma 6.5. For a given $i,j,q$ and associated string that is read by the algorithm in the computation, let the random variable $(q(i,j,q),c(i,j,q))$ denote the state and confidence after the computation $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ . We define the signed confidence, denoted $c^{\pm}(i,j,q)$ , to be defined as $+c(i,j,q)$ if $q(i,j,q)=A(q,x(i:j])$ and $-c(i,j,q)$ otherwise. For intuition, the more positive $c^{\pm}(i,j,q)$ is, the more correct with higher confidence the output $(q(i,j,q),c(i,j,q))$ is, whereas the more negative $c_{\pm}(i,j,q)$ is, the more $q(i,j,q)$ is incorrect with high confidence. So, $c^{\pm}(i,j,q)$ gives us a scaled measure of how correct the output of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ is.

#### Lemma 6.6.

For any $0\leq i<j\leq n$ , $q\in\{0,1\}^{s}$ , and $e\in\mathbb{R}$ , given $\leq\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log(j-i)}{\log n}-e$ fraction of corruptions in the bits read by the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ , we have $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j,q)]>e$ .

We defer the proof to Section 6.2.3 and return to the proof of Lemma 6.5.

#### Proof of Lemma 6.5.

In the special case where $i=0,j=n,q=\emptyset$ and there are $\leq\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}-e<\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log(j-i)}{r}-e$ errors (where the inequality follows because $\log n<\varepsilon\cdot r$ ), by Lemma 6.6 we have that $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(0,n,\emptyset)]>e$ .

Then, the final amplification step of the protocol computes the pair $(q(0,n,\emptyset),c(0,n,\emptyset))$ for $\log^{2}n$ times, where in each chunk $i$ we denote the fraction of error to be $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}-e_{i}\right)$ , where $\sum_{i}e_{i}\geq\frac{\varepsilon\log^{2}n}{2}$ since we assumed the total error was $\leq\frac{1}{4}-\varepsilon$ . Also, the protocol outputs $A(x)$ if and only if $\sum_{i}c^{\pm}_{i}(0,n,\emptyset)$ (denoting the value of $c^{\pm}(0,n,\emptyset)$ in the $i$ ’th chunk) is positive. By Azuma’s inequality,

$$ Pr\left[\sum_{i}c^{\pm}_{i}(0,n,\emptyset)>0\right]\geq Pr\left[\sum_{i}\left(c^{\pm}_{i}(0,n,\emptyset)-e_{i}\right)>-\frac{\varepsilon\log^{2}n}{2}\right]\geq 1-\exp\left(-\frac{\varepsilon^{2}\log^{2}n}{32}\right). $$

∎

Combining Lemmas 6.2, 6.4, and 6.5, this concludes the proof of Theorem 1.1.

#### 6.2.3 Proof of Lemma 6.6

We remark that this section constitutes the main difference in the analysis of Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2. In Algorithm 1, the recursive calls to $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a})$ can be computed in any order, and so $c^{\pm}(i,j)$ is easy to analyze and converges quickly. In Algorithm 2, the recursive call to $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a},q_{a-1})$ has no hope of providing any useful information until $q_{a-1}$ is correct, and so in this algorithm, the quantity $c^{\pm}(i,j,q)$ requires a more careful analysis, and ultimately converges slower.

We prove Lemma 6.6 by induction on $j-i$ . We’ll show the statement for a specific value of $(i,j,q)$ where $j-i$ is a power of $r$ assuming it holds for any $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},q^{\prime})$ where $j^{\prime}-i^{\prime}<j-i$ (and $j^{\prime}-i^{\prime}$ is a power of $r$ ).

We begin with the base case of $j-i=1$ . In this case, the algorithm simply reads (a corrupted version of) $\mathsf{LDC}(x)$ , and by Theorem 4.1, it holds that $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j,q)]>e$ since there is at most $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-e\right)$ error.

Now, suppose we are in the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ . We start with some useful notation.

We say that a state $q^{\prime}_{a}$ is correct when it is equal to the state produced by the algorithm $A$ starting at $q$ and executing steps $i$ to $i_{a}$ (as defined in Line 8 of the algorithm). That is, it is equal to $A(q,x(i:i_{a}])$ . We note that this is different from requiring only $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a},q_{a-1})$ to be done correctly from the starting state $q_{a-1}$ .

In the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ , we say that the output of the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i_{a-1},i_{a},q_{a-1})$ in the $b$ ’th chunk is $(\hat{q}_{a,b},\hat{c}_{a,b})$ . We define the signed confidence $\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}$ to be the confidence $\hat{c}_{a,b}$ signed by whether the guess $\hat{q}_{a,b}$ is correct: that is,

$$ \hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}:=\begin{cases}\hat{c}_{a,b}&\text{$\hat{q}_{a,b}$ is correct}\\
-\hat{c}_{a,b}&\text{$\hat{q}_{a,b}$ is incorrect}.\end{cases} $$

The cumulative best guess and confidence for $A(q,x(i:i_{a}])$ after chunk $b$ , as initialized in Line 9, are denoted by $(q_{a,b},c_{a,b})$ . We let $q_{0,b}=\emptyset$ . We can define a cumulative signed confidence $c^{\pm}_{a,b}$ as follows:

$$ c^{\pm}_{a,b}:=\begin{cases}c_{a,b}&\text{$q_{a,b}$ is correct}\\
-c_{a,b}&\text{$q_{a,b}$ is incorrect}.\end{cases} $$

We first show that $c^{\pm}_{a,b}$ is correct proportional to $\sum_{d\leq b}e_{d}$ assuming that $q_{a-1,b}$ is correct.

#### Lemma 6.7.

Let $a\in[r]$ index the $r$ intervals $(i_{a-1},i_{a}]$ in the computation of $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ . Let each of the $\ell$ chunks in the computation be indexed by $b\in[\ell]$ and suppose chunk $b$ has $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{j-i}{r}}{\log n}-e_{b}\right)$ fraction of corruption. Then, for all $a\in[r]$ , with probability $\geq 1-a\ell^{2}\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{32}\right)$ it holds for all $b\in[\ell]$ that either $c^{\pm}_{a,b}>\sum_{d\leq b}e_{d}-\frac{a\ell}{r\log n}$ or $q_{a-1,b}$ is incorrect.

#### Proof.

We use induction on $a$ . Let us prove the statement for $a$ assuming it is true for $a-1$ . Our base case is $a=0$ , and it holds that $q_{0,b}$ is correct (meaning equal to $q$ ) for all $b\in[\ell]$ .

Fix some chunk $b$ . For $d\leq b$ , we define the altered confidence $\hat{c}^{\mathsf{alt}}_{a,d}$ to be the signed confidence, with a caveat for when $q_{a-1,d-1}$ is incorrect, as follows:

$$ \hat{c}^{\mathsf{alt}}_{a,d}:=\begin{cases}1&\text{$q_{a-1,d-1}$ is incorrect}\\
c^{\pm}_{a,b}&\text{$q_{a-1,d-1}$ is correct}.\end{cases} $$

Then, for any $0\leq b^{\prime}<b$ , the sequence $\left\{X_{b^{\prime},d}:=\sum_{b^{\prime}<d^{\prime}\leq d}\left(\hat{c}^{\mathsf{alt}}_{a,d^{\prime}}-e_{d^{\prime}}\right)\right\}_{b^{\prime}<d\leq b}$ is a submartingale. To see this, we have that $\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{c}^{\mathsf{alt}}_{a,d}\right]\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,d}\right]>e_{d}$ , where the last inequality was by induction on induction on $j-i$ . Furthermore, $|c^{\pm}_{a,d}-e_{d}|\leq 2$ . Then, by Azuma’s inequality,

$$ \Pr\left[X_{b^{\prime},b}\leq-\frac{\ell}{2r\log n}\right]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\ell^{2}}{32r^{2}\log^{2}n(b-b^{\prime})}\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\ell}{32r^{2}\log^{2}n}\right)=\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{32}\right). $$

recalling that $\ell=r^{2}\log^{4}{n}$ . By a union bound,

$$ \Pr\left[X_{b^{\prime},b}>-\frac{\ell}{2r\log n}~~\forall~0\leq b^{\prime}<b\right]\geq 1-\ell\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{32}\right). $$

Now, we return to proving the lemma statement. We have to prove that the statement holds simultaneously for all $b\in[\ell]$ with high probability.

By the inductive hypothesis, Equation (6.2.3), and a union bound, we have that with probability $\geq 1-(a-1)\ell^{2}\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{32}\right)-\ell\cdot\ell\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{32}\right)=1-a\ell^{2}\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{32}\right)$ , the following two conditions simultaneously hold:

- 1. for all $d$ for which $\sum_{d^{\prime}\leq d}e_{d^{\prime}}\geq\frac{(a-1)\ell}{r}$ it holds that $c^{\pm}_{a-1,d}>0$ , or in other words $q_{a-1,d}$ is correct, and

- 2. for all $b\in[\ell]$ , it holds that $X_{b^{\prime},b}>-\frac{\ell}{2r\log n}~~\forall~0\leq b^{\prime}<b$ .

Assume for now that we are not within this failure probability. For any chunk $b$ , let $b^{*}$ be the last chunk $\leq b$ in which $q_{a-1,d}$ changed values. If $q_{a-1,b^{*}}$ is incorrect, then the lemma is proven, because $q_{a-1,b}=q_{a-1,b^{*}}$ is also incorrect. So assume that $q_{a-1,b^{*}}$ is correct.

If $b^{*}=b$ then $c^{\pm}_{a,b}=0$ since $(q_{a,b},c_{a,b})$ was reset to $(\emptyset,0)$ . Moreover, because $q_{a-1,b-1}$ has to be incorrect, we have that $\sum_{d<b}e_{d}<\frac{(a-1)\ell}{r}$ by assumption 1. Then, we have that

$$ c^{\pm}_{a,b}=0>\frac{(a-1)\ell}{r\log n}+1-\frac{a\ell}{r\log n}\geq\sum_{d<b}e_{d}+e_{b}-\frac{a\ell}{r\log n}=\sum_{d\leq b}e_{d}-\frac{a\ell}{r\log n}, $$

as desired, where the first inequality follows because $\ell=r^{2}\log^{4}n>r\log n$ .

Otherwise, $b^{*}<b$ . Then, since $q_{a-1,b^{*}}$ is correct, the value of $q_{a-1,b^{*}-1}$ in chunk $b^{*}-1$ was incorrect, and so $\sum_{d<b^{*}}e_{d}\leq\frac{(a-1)\ell}{r\log n}$ by assumption 1. Since $q_{a-1,d}$ is correct for all $b^{*}\leq d<b$ , we have that $\hat{c}^{\mathsf{alt}}_{a,d}=\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,d}$ for all $b^{*}<d\leq b$ . Moreover, $c^{\pm}_{a,b}\geq\sum_{b^{*}<d\leq b}\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,d}$ . To see this, notice that for all $b$ , it holds that $c^{\pm}_{a,b}-c^{\pm}_{a,b-1}\geq\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,b}$ . Then,

$$ c^{\pm}_{a,b}\geq\sum_{b^{*}<d\leq b}\hat{c}^{\pm}_{a,d}=\sum_{b^{*}<d\leq b}\hat{c}^{\mathsf{alt}}_{a,d}=X_{b^{*},b}+\sum_{b^{*}<d\leq b}e_{d}. $$

Therefore, by Equation (6.2.3),

$$ \displaystyle c^{\pm}_{a,b} \displaystyle=X_{b^{*},b}+\sum_{b^{*}<d\leq b}e_{d} \displaystyle>-\frac{\ell}{2r\log n}+\sum_{d\leq b}e_{d}-e_{b^{*}}-\sum_{d<b^{*}}e_{d} \displaystyle>-\frac{\ell}{2r\log n}+\sum_{d\leq b}e_{d}-1-\frac{(a-1)\ell}{r\log n} \displaystyle>\sum_{d\leq b}e_{d}-\frac{a\ell}{r\log n}. $$

This holds for all $b\in[\ell]$ , as desired. ∎

We now take $b=\ell$ in Lemma 6.7. First, we need a way to reconcile the values of $e$ and $e_{b}$ . Recall that from the statement of Lemma 6.6 that $e$ is defined to be such that there is $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log{j-i}}{\log n}-e\right)$ fraction of error in the bits read by $\mathsf{estA}(i,j,q)$ . In Lemma 6.7, chunk $b$ had $\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{j-i}{r}}{\log n}-e_{b}\right)$ fraction of error. This means that the total fraction of error is equal to

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log(j-i)}{\log n}-e \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\ell}\sum_{b\leq\ell}\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{j-i}{r}}{\log n}-e_{b}\right) \displaystyle\implies e \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\ell}\cdot\sum_{b\leq\ell}e_{b}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log r}{\log n}. $$

#### Lemma 6.8.

With probability at least $1-\frac{1}{n}$ , it holds that for all $a\in[r]$ where $q_{a-1,\ell}$ is correct that $\frac{c^{\pm}_{a,\ell}}{\ell}>e+\frac{1}{\log n}$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 6.7, using a union bound, it holds with probability at least

$$ \displaystyle 1-\sum_{1\leq a\leq r}a\ell^{2}\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{32}\right) \displaystyle\geq 1-r^{2}\ell^{2}\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{32}\right) \displaystyle\geq 1-\ell^{3}\exp\left(-\frac{\log^{2}n}{32}\right) \displaystyle\geq 1-\frac{1}{n} $$

(because $\ell<n$ ) that for all values of $a$ where $q_{a-1,\ell}$ is correct, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{c^{\pm}_{a,\ell}}{\ell} \displaystyle>\frac{\sum_{d\leq\ell}e_{d}-\frac{a\ell}{r\log n}}{\ell} \displaystyle\geq e+\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\frac{\log r}{\log n}-\frac{1}{\log n} \displaystyle\geq e+\frac{1}{\log n} $$

since for sufficiently large $n$ , we have that $\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\cdot\log r>2$ . ∎

We return to the computation of $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j,q)]$ . Note that

$$ c^{\pm}(i,j,q)=\begin{cases}+\min_{a\in[r]}\{\frac{c_{a,\ell}}{\ell}\}&\text{$q_{r}$ is correct}\\
-\min_{a\in[r]}\{\frac{c_{a,\ell}}{\ell}\}&\text{$q_{r}$ is incorrect}.\end{cases} $$

We split the proof of Lemma 6.6 based on whether $e+\frac{1}{\log n}\geq 0$ .

If $e+\frac{1}{\log n}\geq 0$ , define the event $E$ to be the event where $\frac{c^{\pm}_{a,\ell}}{\ell}>e+\frac{1}{\log n}$ for all $a\in[r]$ . We show that $E$ holds with probability at least $1-\frac{1}{n}$ . This is due to Lemma 6.8, which says that with probability $\geq 1-\frac{1}{n}$ , simultaneously for all $a\in[r]$ if $q_{a-1,\ell}$ is correct then $\frac{c^{\pm}_{a,\ell}}{\ell}>e+\frac{1}{n}\geq 0$ . Let $E$ be the event that this holds. Then, since $q_{0,\ell}=q$ is correct by definition, it follows that $q_{a,\ell}$ is correct for all $a\in[r]$ . Since $q_{a-1,\ell}$ is correct for all $a\in[r]$ , it holds that $\frac{c^{\pm}_{a,\ell}}{\ell}>e+\frac{1}{n}$ also. Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j,q)] \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\min_{a\in[r]}\left\{\frac{c_{a,\ell}}{\ell}\right\}\Bigg|E\right]\cdot\Pr[E]+(\text{min value of $c^{\pm}(i,j,q)$})\cdot\left(1-\Pr[E]\right) \displaystyle>\left(e+\frac{1}{\log n}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)+(-1)\cdot\frac{1}{n} \displaystyle=e+\frac{n-e\log{n}-1-\log n}{n\log n} \displaystyle>e. $$

If $e+\frac{1}{\log n}<0$ , then if $q_{r,\ell}$ is correct, then $\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j,q)]\geq 0>e+\frac{1}{\log n}\geq e$ . Otherwise, $q_{r,\ell}$ is incorrect. By Lemma 6.8, with probability $\geq 1-\frac{1}{n}$ , it holds that $\frac{c^{\pm}_{a,\ell}}{\ell}>e+\frac{1}{\log n}$ for all $a$ as long as $q_{a-1,\ell}$ is correct. Let the event this occurs be $E$ . If $q_{r,\ell}$ is incorrect, there is a smallest $a>0$ such that $q_{a,\ell}$ is incorrect (note that $q_{0,\ell}=0$ is always correct), for which it holds that $\frac{c^{\pm}_{a,\ell}}{\ell}>e+\frac{1}{\log n}$ given $E$ . Since $q_{a,\ell}$ is incorrect it holds that $c^{\pm}_{a,\ell}=-c_{a,\ell}$ , implying that $\frac{c_{a,\ell}}{\ell}<-e-\frac{1}{\log n}$ . As such,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[c^{\pm}(i,j,q)] \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\left[-\min_{a\in[r]}\left\{\frac{c_{a,\ell}}{\ell}\right\}\Bigg|E\right]\cdot\Pr[E]+(\text{min value of $c^{\pm}(i,j,q)$})\cdot\left(1-\Pr[E]\right) \displaystyle>\left(e+\frac{1}{\log n}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)+(-1)\cdot\frac{1}{n} \displaystyle=e+\frac{n-e\log{n}-1-\log n}{n\log n} \displaystyle>e. $$

This concludes the proof of Lemma 6.6.

**Authors:** Zhiyang He ††thanks: Email: szhe@mit.edu. Supported by the MIT Department of Mathematics and the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program under Grant No. 2141064. ## Abstract

The development of quantum codes with good error correction parameters and useful sets of transversal gates is a problem of major interest in quantum error correction. Abundant prior works have studied transversal gates which are restricted to acting on all logical qubits simultaneously. In this work, we study codes that support transversal gates which induce addressable logical gates, i.e., the logical gates act on logical qubits of our choice. As we consider scaling to high-rate codes, the study and design of low-overhead, addressable logical operations presents an important problem for both theoretical and practical purposes.

Our primary result is the construction of an explicit qubit code for which any triple of logical qubits across one, two, or three codeblocks can be addressed with a logical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate via a depth-one circuit of physical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates, and whose parameters are asymptotically good, up to polylogarithmic factors. The result naturally generalizes to other gates including the $\mathsf{C}^{\ell}Z$ gates for $\ell\neq 2$ .

Going beyond this, we develop a formalism for constructing quantum codes with addressable and transversal gates. Our framework, called addressable orthogonality, encompasses the original triorthogonality framework of Bravyi and Haah (Phys. Rev. A 2012), and extends this and other frameworks to study addressable gates. We demonstrate the power of this framework with the construction of an asymptotically good qubit code for which pre-designed, pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits within a single codeblock may be addressed with a logical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate via a physical depth-one circuit of $\mathsf{Z}$ , $\mathsf{CZ}$ and $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates. In an appendix, we show that our framework extends to addressable and transversal $T$ gates, up to Clifford corrections.

## 1 Introduction

It is a major challenge in fault-tolerant quantum computation to lower the overhead of quantum error correction [Sho95, Got97, ABO97], that is, the amount by which a quantum circuit must be made larger, both in space and in time, in order to be made fault-tolerant. Significant progress has been made in this area in many directions, although we still notably lack a well-developed theory of quantum codes supporting transversal gates.

The most standard notion of transversality is as follows. We say that a code on $n$ physical qubits encoding $k$ logical qubits supports the single-qubit gate $U$ transversally if, by acting on the physical qubits with the gate $U^{\otimes n}$ , the induced effect on the logical qubits is to execute the gate $U$ on all $k$ encoded qubits, i.e., the gate $\overline{U^{\otimes k}}$ is executed. The point is that acting transversally is an inherently fault-tolerant operation because errors cannot spread within a codeblock. This definition can be extended in a number of directions, particularly when $U$ is a multi-qubit gate. In general, the broadest notion of transversality asks us to perform a non-trivial logical action via a constant-depth circuit.

While transversal gates offer a convenient and low-overhead approach to executing logical gates fault-tolerantly, unfortunately no quantum code can support a universal set of transversal gates [EK09]. It is therefore natural to ask: how can we construct quantum codes with the most flexible and powerful transversal gates, for use in universal fault-tolerant computations?

Substantial effort has been invested in this problem. A pivotal line of research studies transversal gates on topological codes, notably the color codes on cellulated surfaces. The two-dimensional color codes [BMD06], of which the classic 7-qubit Steane code [CS96, Ste96] is the smallest instance, support the entire set of Clifford gates transversally. Higher-dimensional color codes support transversal non-Clifford gates in higher levels of the Clifford hierarchy, notably the $T$ gate [Bom15, KB15] and the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate [PR13, KYP15]. A transversal $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate has also been constructed in 3D surface codes [VB19]. These results led to fault-tolerant schemes which perform universal gates by code-switching between 2D and 3D topological codes [Bom16, VB19].

Another line of research studies algebraic constructions of quantum codes with transversal non-Clifford gates for use in magic state distillation (MSD) [BK05] protocols. MSD is a central yet expensive technique that consumes low fidelity magic states to produce high fidelity magic states, which can be used in gate teleportation protocols [GC99] to perform universal fault-tolerant computation. By improving the error-correction parameters of the code used, we can obtain more efficient MSD schemes [BK05, CAB12, BH12, KT19]. In recent works, asymptotically good quantum codes supporting non-Clifford transversal gates were constructed [WHY24, GG24, Ngu24], which implies constant-overhead MSD protocols for qubits [WHY24].11 1 Here, the meaning of the word “overhead” refers only to the ratio of inputted to outputted magic states, not to the spacetime-overhead of the scheme, as is relevant in a full fault-tolerant quantum computing protocol. We note that [NP24] constructed a MSD protocol with low spacetime overhead using algebraic codes.

Complementary to developments through algebraic methods, a novel line of recent research, inspired by the line of work which led to asymptotically good quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes [HHO21, PK21b, BE21a, PK22, LZ22, DHLV23], studies construction of qLDPC codes with transversal non-Clifford gates through homological methods [ZSP+23, SPW24, GL24, Lin24, HKZ24, BDET24, Zhu25]. The codes constructed in these works are not asymptotically good, but have constant or poly-logarithmic stabilizer check weight, which is amenable to potential applications in fault-tolerant schemes.

#### A new goal: Addressability.

Almost all transversal gates constructed in aforementioned works act globally on the logical spaces: a constant depth physical circuit induces a non-trivial logical action on all or a large portion of the logical qubits. For codes which encode a single logical qubit, such as the surface code or simple instances of 2D color codes, these gates are exactly what’s needed to build fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols. For high-rate codes which encode many logical qubits, such control over the logical information is too coarse for applications outside of MSD; there are only limited situations in which it is algorithmically useful to execute the same gate on every qubit (except perhaps the Hadamard gate). Instead, what we really want is for the code to support transversal gates that are also addressable. What this means is that, given any logical qubit indexed by $A$ , there is some constant depth physical circuit, perhaps acting on a subset of the physical qubits, such that the induced logical gate acts only on the $A$ ’th logical qubit. Such fine-grained logical control is especially useful for implementation of generic algorithms, e.g. arithmetic circuits like the quantum adder [Gid18].

We observe that this is a common limitation that goes even beyond the works discussed. For high-rate quantum codes, notably quantum LDPC codes, it is often difficult to act on an individual logical qubit without acting on the rest of the logical space. In existing fault-tolerant schemes based on constant-rate QLDPC codes [Got13, FGL20, TKY24, NP24], logical gates are performed by full-block gate teleportation [GC99, Kni05]. For specific codes, existing studies on transversal or constant-depth gates, notably those based on automorphisms [CRSS98, GR13, BCG+24, ES24, SKW+24] and other code symmetries [RCP19, HLC21, WQB23, QWV23, BB24], also primarily concern operations on the full logical space. Two general techniques which inherently address individual logical qubits are pieceable fault-tolerance [YTC16] and generalized code surgery [CKBB22];22 2 Generalized code surgery is a form of code deformation [BMD09, VB22], which has been applied to design addressable logical action on high rate codes [BVC+17, KP21]. A different yet similar technique is homomorphic measurement [HJOY23], which was utilized in a recent work [XZZ+24] to design addressable logical action on hypergraph product codes. As in the case of surgery, these proposals incur more overhead than constant depth unitary circuits, i.e., transversal circuits. the overhead of the latter was significantly improved in recent works [CHRY24, Cow24, WY24, IGND24, SJOY24, ZL24]. Nevertheless, these techniques are still much more costly when compared to constant-depth circuits, i.e., transversal circuits.

For these reasons, we believe the study and design of low-overhead, addressable logical operations on high-rate quantum codes is an interesting problem for both theoretical and practical purposes. Theoretically, recent works on constructing codes with transversal gates have opened many new possibilities for code and fault-tolerant scheme designs. Practically, recent experimental progress has demonstrated sub-threshold scaling of the surface code [AI23, AABA+24] and logical operations on 2D color codes [RRJ+24, LBH+24]. As we consider scaling to codes that encode a growing number of qubits in every block, notably quantum LDPC codes with promising finite-length performances [TZ13, LTZ15, BE21b, PK21a, BCG+24, XBAP+24, LP24], addressable logic is not only a natural question to study, but also critical for practical efficiency.

In this paper, we construct the first quantum codes to support transversal, addressable non-Clifford gates, such as the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate, and we obtain such codes that are near-asymptotically good (for the strongest sense of addressability) or asymptotically good (for weaker senses of addressability). As far as we know, transversal and addressable non-Clifford gates have not been established for any quantum code, except in a particular weak sense that we discuss below and in Section 2.2. While we construct codes that are (near) asymptotically good, our codes are not LDPC.33 3 Note that transversal, addressable Clifford operations have been studied on LDPC codes in [ZSP+23, HKZ24]. We believe that the results demonstrated in the present paper can provide important ideas for similar developments on LDPC codes.

### 1.1 Our Results

#### Near-asymptotically good code with addressable non-Clifford gates.

Our primary result will be concerned with the strongest (and most computationally useful) form of addressability. Here, we will look to construct codes for which any triple of logical qudits within one, two, or three blocks of the code may be addressed with the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate via a depth-one circuit of physical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates. We say that gates on codes satisfying this strong form of addressability are addressable.

#### Theorem 1.1.

There exists an explicit family of quantum CSS codes over qubits with parameters

$$ \left[\left[n,\Omega\left(\frac{n}{\text{polylog}(n)}\right),\Omega\left(\frac{n}{\text{polylog}(n)}\right)\right]\right]_{2} $$

supporting a transversal, addressable $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate. Specifically, any three logical qubits across one, two, or three blocks of the code may be addressed with a logical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate via a depth-one circuit of physical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates.

We note that this code has asymptotically optimal error correction parameters up to polylogarithmic factors, and this statement will be proved using the results of Sections 3 and 6. We also remark that the same result may be obtained for any $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gate, not just for $\ell=3$ , and even for more complicated diagonal gates with entries $\pm 1$ on the diagonal, as we will describe. For practical purposes, we note that a depth-1 physical circuit of $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates can be naturally realized on platforms based on neutral atoms, which have undergone exciting recent development [BEG+24], by arranging atoms into the desired triples and applying a single laser pulse to induce the required multi-qubit interaction [LKS+19, EBK+23].

There is an important piece of folklore that a code supporting a transversal gate in the $\ell$ -th level of the Clifford hierarchy supports a transversal and addressable gate in the $(\ell-1)$ -th level of the Clifford hierarchy [HKZ24, Lin24, BDET24]. This notion is indeed true for single-qubit gates, but in the case of multi-qubit gates such as $\mathsf{CCZ}$ , the resulting form of addressability is limited to certain triples of qubits and is thus much weaker and less computationally useful than what we establish in Theorem 1.1. We discuss this in more detail in Section 2.2.

Given the stringent structure required on the codes to achieve the above result, we prove this using very specialized properties of certain algebraic codes, namely classical Reed-Solomon (RS) codes. Indeed, using the “matrix-to-quantum code” construction [BH12, KT19, WHY24] to construct a quantum code from the generator matrix of a classical code, in this case an RS code, one obtains the above result for qudits of dimension $q=2^{t}$ , as will be done in Section 3. Then, using the qudit-to-qubit conversions of Section 6, which are an application of results in [Ngu24, GG24],44 4 Note that the qudit-to-qubit conversions of [WHY24] are too weak for the present work, and we exclusively use those of [Ngu24, GG24]. we obtain Theorem 1.1 for qubits. It is conceptually important to note that, being made from Reed-Solomon codes, the qudit codes in this construction are asymptotically good, but only over qudits of growing size, i.e., $2^{t}=q\sim n$ , where $n$ is the length of the code. This means the polylogarithmic factors are lost in the conversion to qubit codes in Section 6. By contrast, constructions from algebraic geometry (AG) codes in this paper may be made asymptotically good over a constant field size, i.e., $q=2^{t}=\Theta(1)$ , meaning that the corresponding qubit codes are also asymptotically good. Obtaining the addressability of the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate with AG codes appears to be considerably more involved than with RS codes, however, this does appear to be a promising avenue to obtain Theorem 1.1 with asymptotically good parameters; this direction is deferred to future work.

#### A framework for transversal addressable gates.

Much of the progress on constructing codes with transversal non-Clifford gates stems from the establishment of frameworks that reduce the task of constructing codes with non-Clifford gates to the task of constructing classical codes satisfying certain properties. The first such framework was the notion of triorthogonal matrices, with the corresponding triorthogonal quantum codes supporting transversal $T$ gates up to Clifford correction [BH12]. This framework has gone on to be highly influential in quantum coding theory [ecz24], and has been extended for prime-dimensional qudits [KT19] and for prime-power-dimensional qudits [WHY24].55 5 While the basis of knowledge on a quantum code’s properties that are necessary (not only sufficient) for supporting various transversal gates is incomplete, it is known [RCNP20] that triorthogonality is also necessary for a quantum code to support a transversal $T$ gate. We feel that such necessity statements on triorthogonality-like frameworks should be generalizable to other gates and other qudits. In Section 4, we develop a natural generalization of Bravyi and Haah’s triorthogonality framework, and those that follows it, to addressable non-Clifford gates which we call addressable orthogonality (see Section 4.1 for a precise definition). One consequence of this framework is that it allows us to construct codes supporting the transversal addressability of a large family of diagonal gates. The first demonstration of the power and flexibility of this formalism comes in the form of our second main result, which is as follows.

#### Theorem 1.2.

There exists an explicit family of (asymptotically good) qubit CSS codes with parameters

$$ \left[\left[n,\Theta(n),\Theta(n)\right]\right]_{2}, $$

supporting a addressable and transversal $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate on pre-designed (pairwise disjoint) intra-block triples of logical qubits. Specifically, the logical qubits in one block of the code are partitioned into sets of three, and one may address any such set with the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate via a depth-one circuit of physical $\mathsf{Z}$ , $\mathsf{CZ}$ and $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates.

We call this notion pre-designed addressability since the code supports gate actions on arbitrary, but pre-designed, intra-block triples of qubits. This result is proved in Sections 4, 5, and 6 and instantiates part of our addressable orthogonality framework with algebraic geometry codes. As mentioned, since these codes may be instantiated to be asymptotically good over fixed-size qudits, i.e., over a fixed field of size $q=2^{t}$ with $t=O(1)$ , the qubit codes resulting from the conversions in Section 6 are also asymptotically good.

We provide two further demonstrations of the flexibility of our addressable orthogonality formalism.

- 1. In Appendix A, we show that one of our addressable orthogonality notions can lead to the construction of quantum codes with transversal, addressable $T$ gates, up to the application of corrective Cliffords. Since this so naturally extends the original framework of Bravyi and Haah, we give it the name addressable triorthogonality. However, we do not have an instantiation in mind.

- 2. In other parts of Section 4 and 5, we go beyond the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate and thoroughly explore other gates with entries $\pm 1$ on the diagonal in the Clifford hierarchy,66 6 Note that the qualification “in the Clifford hierarchy” is technically redundant for such gates. including, but not limited to $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates for $\ell>3$ . It is convenient to describe such gates using the Galois qudit formalism, where a $q=2^{t}$ -dimensional qudit is described by computational basis states labeled by elements of the corresponding finite field $\left\{\ket{\eta}\right\}_{\eta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}}$ . Note that, despite being larger qudits, they are still of interest, since a $q=2^{t}$ -dimensional qudit is equivalent to a set of $t$ qubits, as will be shown in the preliminary material of Section 2.3.77 7 Further relevant preliminaries are discussed in Sections 2.1 and 2.2. Then, the set of gates $U_{q,\ell}^{\beta}$ , where $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ defined via

$$ U_{q,\ell}^{\beta}\ket{\eta}=\exp\left(i\pi\tr(\beta\eta^\ell)\right)\ket{\eta}, $$

(3) where $\tr:\mathbb{F}_{q}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}$ is the trace linear map (see Section 2.1), is an important set of gates since they can generate any diagonal gate with $\pm 1$ on the diagonal for $q=2^{t}$ -dimensional qudits, and therefore also for qubits, as will be discussed in Appendix B. We will discuss how quantum codes may be designed supporting these gates (and their qubit versions) addressably, leading to quantum codes whose addressability properties may be highly tailored to particular situations. We also show that the methods following from our addressable orthogonality framework are actually strictly stronger than what may be achieved using the folklore intuition described above, in that they may lead to strictly stronger parameters. In particular, one of the surprising results we obtain is that, by using Reed-Solomon codes, one can obtain as good asymptotic code parameters with transversal and addressable gates as with merely transversal gates; this result is captured by Theorem 5.5. We will discuss this more in the introduction to Section 5.

### 1.2 Discussion and Further Directions

In this work, we have initiated the study of quantum codes supporting transversal, addressable non-Clifford gates. This naturally leads to a large number of well-motivated research directions of theoretical and practical importance.

#### Open Problem 1:

Does there exist an asymptotically good qubit code supporting a transversal, addressable $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate? As previously mentioned, a natural approach to this would be to leverage the internal structure of algebraic geometry codes in a similar way to how we have leveraged the internal structure of Reed-Solomon codes in this work. We look forward to pursuing this in future work.

The next natural question concerns the stabilizer weight of codes with transversal, addressable gates.

#### Open Problem 2:

What are the best achievable asymptotic (and practical) parameters for a quantum LDPC code supporting a multi-qubit transversal non-Clifford gate, such as the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate? Can we achieve addressability in addition? It is interesting to ask if the ideas on addressability contained herein apply to recent transversality constructions such as [GL24], or to any future constructions. Of course, one may ask the same questions for non-LDPC codes, where the interest would be in the actual constants of rate and relative distance.

It is worth emphasizing that the recent works mentioned primarily focus on diagonal non-Clifford gates with entries $\pm 1$ on the diagonal. Quantum codes directly supporting other non-Clifford gates, such as the $T$ gate, transversally (addressably), or even transversally up to Clifford corrections as in the triorthogonal codes [BH12] are still not known to exist with particularly good parameters.

#### Open Problem 3:

What are the best achievable asymptotic parameters for a quantum code supporting a single-qubit non-Clifford gate, such as the $T$ gate, transversally? What if we require that the code is LDPC, the gate is addressable, or if we allow Clifford corrections?

In this direction, we present the notion of addressable triorthogonality (from which one can obtain transversal, addressable $T$ gates up to Clifford corrections) in Appendix A, which naturally generalizes Bravyi and Haah’s original notion of triorthogonality [BH12]. However, we do not have an instantiation. We hope that further work will help to address the following problem.

#### Open Problem 4:

Can we instantiate the addressable triorthogonality notion presented in Appendix A to make quantum codes with addressable, transversal $T$ gates, up to Clifford corrections? Is it possible to obtain well-performing small examples of such codes in a similar way to how [JA24] does with the usual triorthogonal (as well as doubly even and weak triple even) quantum codes?

Besides code constructions, it would also be useful to understand and characterize the necessary, as well as the sufficient conditions for quantum codes to support interesting addressable and transversal gates.

#### Open Problem 5:

Can we characterize necessary, as well as sufficient conditions for certain codes to support general (diagonal) gates in the Clifford hierarchy (addressably) transversally, beyond just the $T$ gate [RCNP20, HLC22]? Could the addressable orthogonality framework in this paper offer insight to this?

Furthermore, the main motivation behind studying powerful transversal gates is to lower the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation. Given the addressable non-Clifford gates in our constructions, there are many potential approaches to realize universal fault-tolerance. One idea is to use surgery techniques to measure Pauli observables on logical qubits. These logical measurements can be used to implement Clifford gates directly on a code, or prepare stabilizer resource states which when teleported into a code translates to a Clifford circuit. In particular, the parallel surgery system of [CHWY25] and the extractor system of [HCWY25], which builds upon the works of [CHRY24, WY24, SJOY24], are both capable of preparing arbitrary Clifford resource states on arbitrary CSS codes. This enables us to teleport a potentially deep and convoluted Clifford circuit into a code with addressable and low-overhead non-Clifford gates, completing a proposal for universal fault-tolerant computation. We leave the cost analysis of this surgery approach, as well as the exploration of other approaches, as interesting open problems for future works.

#### Open Problem 6:

How can we utilize codes with transversal and addressable non-Clifford gates in a fault-tolerant, universal quantum computation scheme?

Finally, a question in a related but somewhat different direction: this paper focuses on implementing diagonal gates with entries $\pm 1$ on the diagonal (which are exactly all diagonal Clifford hierarchy gates with entries $\pm 1$ on the diagonal). Now, the diagonal Clifford hierarchy has been classified [CGK17] for prime-dimensional qudits, and given the equivalence between a $p^{t}$ -dimensional qudit and a set of $t$ $p$ -dimensional qudits, the diagonal Clifford hierarchy for prime-power-dimensional qudits has effectively also been classified. However, it would be very useful and interesting to further characterize the diagonal Clifford hierarchies for prime-power-dimensional qudits in terms of notation that is native to them. This would be of use in the present line of work [WHY24, GG24, Ngu24, GL24] for which algebraic constructions for prime-power qudits based on finite fields enable the construction of qubit codes supporting transversal gates. For example, as we discuss in Appendix B, the diagonal Clifford hierarchy for a $p$ -dimensional qudit may be generated from gates of the form

$$ \sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\exp\left[\frac{2\pi i}{p^{m}}\text{poly}(j)\right]\ket{j}\bra{j} $$

and the level of the Clifford hierarchy always increases with the degree of the polynomial [CGK17]. On the other hand, the diagonal Clifford hierarchy for $2^{t}$ -dimensional qudits with $\pm 1$ on the diagonal may be generated by gates of the form

$$ \sum_{\eta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}}\exp\left[i\pi\tr(\text{poly}(\eta))\right]\ket{\eta}\bra{\eta}, $$

(see Appendix B). The essential point here is that the level of the Clifford hierarchy does not necessarily increase with the degree of the polynomial here, and behaves somewhat erratically. We believe that while the diagonal Clifford hierarchy has been classified, it is both theoretically interesting and important for the design of codes supporting interesting transversal and addressable gates to classify the prime-power-dimensional diagonal Clifford hierarchy in terms of notation akin to (5).

#### Open Problem 7:

Can we understand the diagonal Clifford hierarchy of prime-power-dimensional qudits in a way that is more native to these qudits?

### 1.3 Outline

Preliminary material will be presented in Section 2. The construction of a qudit code via an addressable $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate via Reed-Solomon codes will be made in Section 3. In Section 4, we will introduce the framework of addressable orthogonality and show how it can be used to construct codes with single-qudit addressable gates or single-index addressable multi-qudit gates. Instantiations of the addressable orthogonality framework will be presented in Section 5. Finally, in Section 6, the main results of the paper, which are the qubit code constructions, will be proved via certain qudit-to-qubit conversions.

In Appendix A, we discuss how the addressable orthogonality framework can encapsulate a transversal, addressable $T$ gate; a notion which we call addressable triorthogonality as it directly extends the original triorthogonality framework of Bravyi and Haah [BH12]. In Appendix B, we provide a discussion of the gates primarily considered in this paper in light of the diagonal Clifford hierarchy for qudits of prime-power dimension.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Finite Fields, Qudits and CSS Codes

Given a prime power $q=p^{t}$ , there is exactly one field of order $q$ , up to isomorphism, denoted $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , whose set of non-zero elements in denoted $\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}$ . Throughout the paper, arithmetic will take place in the relevant finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , unless otherwise specified. The field $\mathbb{F}_{q_{1}}$ , where $q_{1}=p_{1}^{t_{1}}$ contains a copy of $\mathbb{F}_{q_{2}}$ , where $q_{2}=p_{2}^{t_{2}}$ , as a subfield if and only if $p_{1}=p_{2}$ and $t_{2}$ divides $t_{1}$ . In particular, $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ contains a copy of the field $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ as a subfield. There is a canonical $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -linear map $\tr_{\mathbb{F}_{q}/\mathbb{F}_{p}}:\mathbb{F}_{q}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}$ defined as

$$ \tr_{\mathbb{F}_{q}/\mathbb{F}_{p}}(\gamma)=\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}\gamma^{p^{i}}. $$

It is a non-obvious yet standard fact that the right-hand side must be in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ [LN96]. This map is known as the trace and may simply be denoted $\tr$ when the domain and range are clear.

Finite fields give us a convenient way to describe qudits of prime-power dimension, as well as their Pauli operations and Clifford hierarchies. Letting $q=p^{t}$ , the state space of a $q$ -dimensional qudit is $\mathbb{C}^{q}$ . Denoting computational basis states as $\{\ket{\eta}:\eta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\}$ , we define Pauli operators $X^{\beta}$ and $Z^{\beta}$ for every $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ via

$$ \displaystyle X^{\beta}\ket{\eta}=\ket{\eta+\beta}\hskip 7.22743pt\mbox{and}\hskip 7.22743ptZ^{\beta}=\omega^{\tr(\beta\eta)}\ket{\eta}, $$

where $\omega$ is a $p$ -th root of unity. In these equations, arithmetic takes place over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ . One may check the commutation relation

$$ X^{\beta}Z^{\gamma}=\omega^{\tr(\beta\gamma)}Z^{\gamma}X^{\beta}. $$

The Pauli group over one qudit is defined as

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{1,q}=\{\omega^{a}X^{\beta}Z^{\gamma},a\in[p],\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\} $$

and the $n$ -qudit Pauli group is defined as $\mathcal{P}_{n,q}=\mathcal{P}_{1,q}^{\otimes n}$ . The Clifford hierarchy was first introduced in [GC99] and has an important role in the field of fault-tolerant quantum computation, being intimately related to the fault-tolerant implementability and distillability of certain gates. It is constructed as follows.

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{n,q}^{(1)} \displaystyle=\mathcal{P}_{n,q} \displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{n,q}^{(k)} \displaystyle=\{U\in U((C^{q})^{\otimes n}):UPU^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{P}_{n,q}\text{ for all }P\in\mathcal{C}_{n,q}^{(k-1)}\}\text{ for }k>1. $$

Notice in particular that $\mathcal{C}_{n,q}^{(2)}$ denotes the Clifford group, and may be written more briefly as simply $\mathcal{C}_{n,q}$ .

The Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code formalism extends to qudits as well. For a vector $\Gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ , we denote $X^{\Gamma}:=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}X^{\Gamma_{i}}$ and $Z^{\Gamma}:=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}Z^{\Gamma_{i}}$ .

#### Definition 2.1 (CSS Codes).

Given two classical $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ -linear codes $\mathcal{L}_{X},\mathcal{L}_{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ satisfying $\mathcal{L}_{X}\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\perp}$ , we define the quantum code space $\textsc{css}(X,\mathcal{L}_{X};Z,\mathcal{L}_{Z})\subseteq(\mathbb{C}^{q})^{\otimes n}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{Q}=\textsc{css}(X,\mathcal{L}_{X};Z,\mathcal{L}_{Z})=\{\ket{\psi}\in(\mathbb{C}^{q})^{\otimes n}:X^{\mathbf{x}}\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi},Z^{\mathbf{z}}\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi}\text{ for all }\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{L}_{X},\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{L}_{Z}\}. $$

We cite some standard facts about CSS codes, and refer readers to proofs in [Got24]. The CSS codespace $\textsc{css}(X,\mathcal{L}_{X};Z,\mathcal{L}_{Z})$ has dimension $k=n-\dim(\mathcal{L}_{X})-\dim(\mathcal{L}_{Z})$ , and it encodes $k$ qudits into $n$ qudits, i.e., it identifies the state space of $k$ qudits, $(\mathbb{C}^{q})^{\otimes k}$ , with some subspace of $(\mathbb{C}^{q})^{\otimes n}$ , called the codepsace. Given the stabilisers specified by $\mathcal{L}_{X}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{Z}$ , the logical $X$ operators are established by making some choice of basis $\{g^{1},\cdots,g^{k}\}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ for the space $\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\perp}/\mathcal{L}_{X}$ .88 8 Normally, when we say that the set $\{g^{1},\ldots,g^{k}\}$ forms a basis for a subspace, we mean that the vectors are in that subspace, they span the space, and no non-trivial linear combination of them sums to zero, i.e., they are linearly independent. Here, saying $\{g^{1},\ldots,g^{k}\}$ form a basis for the space $\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\perp}/\mathcal{L}_{X}$ means that these vectors are in $\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\perp}$ , any coset in this quotient space may be written as a linear combination of cosets of the form $g^{i}+\mathcal{L}_{X}$ , and that no non-trivial linear combination of the $g^{i}$ sums to an element of $\mathcal{L}_{X}$ , i.e., no non-trivial linear combination of cosets of the form $g^{i}+\mathcal{L}_{X}$ sums to the trivial coset. Then, given a vector $u\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{k}$ , the logical encoding of the $k$ -qudit computation basis state labelled by $u$ in the code $\mathcal{Q}$ is, up to normalization,

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\ket{u}}\propto\sum_{g\in\mathcal{L}_{X}}\Ket{\sum_{a=1}^{k}u_{a}g^{a}+g}. $$

From here, it can be checked that $X^{\beta g^{a}}$ is the logical operator $X^{\beta}$ acting on the $a$ ’th logical qudit. We can also find $\{h^{b}\in\mathcal{L}_{X}^{\perp}\setminus\mathcal{L}_{Z}\}_{b\in[k]}$ such that $g^{a}\cdot h^{b}=\bm{1}_{a=b}$ , in which case the $Z^{\gamma}$ logical operator of the $a$ -th logical qubit would be $Z^{\gamma h^{a}}$ . We can check that these operators have the desired commutation relations.

$$ \displaystyle X^{\beta g^{a}}Z^{\gamma h^{b}} \displaystyle=\omega^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tr(\beta\gamma g^a_ih^b_i)}Z^{\gamma h^{b}}X^{\beta g^{a}} \displaystyle=\omega^{\tr(\sum_{i=1}^n \beta\gamma g^a_ih^b_i)}Z^{\gamma h^{b}}X^{\beta g^{a}} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\omega^{\tr(\beta\gamma)}Z^{\gamma h^{b}}X^{\beta g^{a}}&a=b\\
Z^{\gamma h^{b}}X^{\beta g^{a}}&a\not=b.\end{cases} $$

We note explicitly that the summation can be brought inside the trace in equation (15) because $\tr(\cdot)$ is a $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -linear function and $\omega$ is a $p$ -th root of unity.

For a vector $g\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ , we denote its Hamming weight as $|g|$ . For a classical linear code $\mathcal{L}$ , we let $d(\mathcal{L})$ denote its distance, which is $d(\mathcal{L})=\min_{g\in\mathcal{L}\setminus\{0\}}|g|$ .

#### Definition 2.2.

For the quantum CSS code $\mathcal{Q}=\textsc{css}(X,\mathcal{L}_{X};Z,\mathcal{L}_{Z})$ , we define its $X$ distance to be $d_{X}=d(\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\perp}/\mathcal{L}_{X})$ ,99 9 Technically, the quotient space $\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\perp}/\mathcal{L}_{X}$ contains elements of the form $g+\mathcal{L}_{X}$ , and we say that $|g+\mathcal{L}_{X}|=\min_{g^{\prime}\in g+\mathcal{L}_{X}}|g^{\prime}|$ . and its $Z$ distance to be $d_{Z}=d(\mathcal{L}_{X}^{\perp}/\mathcal{L}_{Z})$ . The distance of $\mathcal{Q}$ is $d(\mathcal{Q})=\min(d_{X},d_{Z})$ .

#### Corollary 2.3.

Note that for a CSS code, $d_{X}=d(\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\perp}/\mathcal{L}_{X})\geqslant d(\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\perp})$ , and similarly $d_{Z}\geqslant d(\mathcal{L}_{X}^{\perp})$ . Therefore $d(\mathcal{Q})\geqslant\min(d(\mathcal{L}_{X}^{\perp}),d(\mathcal{L}_{Z}^{\perp}))$ .

We say that $\mathcal{Q}$ is a $[[n,k,d]]_{q}$ quantum code when it encodes $k$ logical qudits (of dimension $q$ ) into $n$ physical qudits, and has distance $d$ . A family of quantum codes with a divergent number of physical qudits $n$ is called asymptotically good if $k,d=\Theta(n)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ .

### 2.2 Non-Clifford Gates and Addressability

In this work, we consider the case $p=2$ (although our results naturally generalise to larger primes $p$ ) and study diagonal non-Clifford gates over qubits and qudits of dimension $q=2^{t}$ . Given that qubits are of much greater practical relevance than larger qudits, we find it necessary to emphasise here that $2^{t}$ -dimensional qudits are still practically interesting because such a qudit is equivalent to a set of $t$ qubits, as will be shown in Section 2.3. Packaging multiple qubits into a single prime-power qudit in this way is a convenient means to describe Clifford hierarchy gates on multiple qubits. In addition, by building quantum codes over qudits, we will convert them to qubit codes in Section 6.

The first and most important non-Clifford gate for our purposes is the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate which acts on 3 qudits of dimension $q$ . This is defined via

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{CCZ}_{q}\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\ket{\eta_{3}} \displaystyle=\exp(i\pi\tr(\eta_1\eta_2\eta_3))\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\ket{\eta_{3}}, $$

or, more generally, given $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{CCZ}_{q}^{\beta}\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\ket{\eta_{3}} \displaystyle=\exp(i\pi\tr(\beta\eta_1\eta_2\eta_3))\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\ket{\eta_{3}}. $$

We note that, here and further on, while the trace is a canonical linear map from $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ to $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ , no generality is lost by using it exclusively, because any linear map $\theta:\mathbb{F}_{q}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}$ may be written as $\theta(\eta)=\tr(\beta\eta)$ for some $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ [LN96]. We also consider the more general $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates, which act on $l$ qudits as

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}_{q}\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\cdots\ket{\eta_{\ell}} \displaystyle=\exp(i\pi\tr(\eta_1\eta_2\cdots\eta_\ell))\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\cdots\ket{\eta_{\ell}}, \displaystyle\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}_{q}^{\beta}\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\cdots\ket{\eta_{\ell}} \displaystyle=\exp(i\pi\tr(\beta\eta_1\eta_2\cdots\eta_\ell))\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\cdots\ket{\eta_{\ell}}. $$
