We conclude this section by proving that any polynomial gate $U_{q,P}^{\beta}$ , as defined in Section 2.2, can be supported single-index addressably on $\mathcal{Q}$ assuming the strong addressable orthogonal property for $G$ . Such gates form an extremely flexible set, and are in fact complete for the set of diagonal qudit Clifford hierarchy gates with entries $\pm 1$ on the diagonal (see Appendix B).

Indeed, let $P$ be an $e$ -variate polynomial of degree- $\ell$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ . We make the following definition as in the case of $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates.

#### Definition 4.13 (Single-index Inter-block Polynomial Gates).

For vectors $h^{1},\cdots,h^{e}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ , for $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ and address $A\in[n]$ , we denote the single-index $U_{P}^{\beta}$ gate acting on qudit $A$ as

$$ \displaystyle U_{P}^{\beta}[A]\ket{h^{1}}\cdots\ket{h^{e}}=\exp(i\pi\tr( \beta P(h^1_A, \cdots, h^e_A)))\ket{h^{1}}\cdots\ket{h^{e}}. $$

For a vector $\Gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ , we denote $U_{P}^{\Gamma}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}U_{P}^{\Gamma_{i}}[i]$ .

Let $G$ and the quantum code $\mathcal{Q}$ be defined as in Section 2.4. For a general polynomial $P$ of degree $\ell$ , we now require the strongly addressable $\ell$ -orthogonality, as follows.

#### Theorem 4.14.

Suppose $G$ has the strong addressable $\ell$ -orthogonality property with respect to $\tau$ . Then for all $A\in[k],\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\overline{U_{P}^{\beta\tau_{A}}[A]}=U_{P}^{\beta\Gamma^{A}}, $$

with $\Gamma^{A}$ as in Equation (82), in the associated quantum code $\mathcal{Q}$ . In words, we can address the $A$ -th logical qudits in the $e$ code blocks with a logical $U_{P}$ gate by acting transversally on the physical qudits.

The proof of this theorem follows essentially the same argument as in those of Theorems 4.6.

#### Proof.

As in the proofs of Theorems 4.6 and 4.7,we start by consider a set of logical computational basis states of $\mathcal{Q}$ : $\overline{\ket{u_{1}}},\cdots,\overline{\ket{u_{e}}}$ . We also consider vectors $f^{(1)},\ldots,f^{(e)}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle f^{(p)}=\sum_{a=1}^{m}u_{a}^{(p)}g^{a} $$

for some $u_{a}^{(p)}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ . Then, we have

$$ \displaystyle U_{P}^{\beta\Gamma^{A}}\ket{f^{(1)}}\ldots\ket{f^{(e)}} \displaystyle=\exp\left(i\pi\tr(\beta\sum_{i=1}^n\Gamma_i^AP(f_i^{(1)}, \ldots, f_i^{(e)}))\right)\ket{f^{(1)}}\ldots\ket{f^{(e)}}. $$

Now we may write

$$ P(f_{i}^{(1)},\ldots,f_{i}^{(e)})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{monomials $T$}\\
\deg(T)\leqslant\ell\end{subarray}}c_{T}T(f_{i}^{(1)},\ldots,f_{i}^{(e)}) $$

for some coefficients $c_{T}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , and using the strong addressable $\ell$ -orthogonality with respect to $\tau$ , we have, for any monomial $T$ of degree less than $\ell$ ,

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma_{i}^{A}T(f_{i}^{(1)},\ldots,f_{i}^{(e)})=\tau_{A}T(u_{A}^{(1)},\ldots,u_{A}^{(e)}). $$

This means that

$$ \displaystyle U_{P}^{\beta\Gamma^{A}}\ket{f^{(1)}}\ldots\ket{f^{(e)}}=\exp\left(i\pi\tr(\beta\tau_AP(u_A^{(1)}, \ldots, u_A^{(e)}))\right)\ket{f^{(1)}}\ldots\ket{f^{(e)}} $$

and, considering the forms of the logical computational basis states $\overline{\ket{u_{p}}}$ , as given in Equation (88), by linearity this implies that

$$ \displaystyle U_{P}^{\beta\Gamma^{A}}\overline{\ket{u_{1}}\ldots\ket{u_{e}}} \displaystyle=\exp\left(i\pi\tr(\beta\tau_AP(u_A^{(1)}, \ldots, u_A^{(e)}))\right)\overline{\ket{u_{1}}\ldots\ket{u_{e}}} \displaystyle=\overline{U_{P}^{\beta\tau_{A}}[A]\ket{u_{1}}\ldots\ket{u_{e}}}, $$

as required. ∎

#### Remark 4.15.

One situation in which the strong addressable $\ell$ -orthogonality is not required is the case of a homogeneous polynomial $P$ . Indeed, if $P$ is a degree- $\ell$ such polynomial, then the conclusion of Theorem 4.14 holds even if $G$ is only addressable $\ell$ -orthogonal.

## 5 Instantiations of the Addressable Orthogonality Framework

We have seen in the previous section how matrices with various addressable orthogonality properties can give rise to quantum codes supporting interesting addressable transversal gates. We will now see how such matrices naturally arise as the generator matrices for punctured classical codes satisfying a multiplication property defined below. Indeed, in Definition 5.1, we will define a regular, and strong $\ell$ -multiplication property, and we will go on to see in Lemma 5.3 that if the classical code $C$ has each property, then the resulting generator matrix for the punctured code has the regular, and strong $\ell$ -orthogonality property, respectively. Note that this multiplication property, and similar properties, have been well-studied in coding theory [Ran15], and it is well-known that codes built from the evaluation of certain functions, such as Reed-Solomon and algebraic geometry codes, naturally satisfy such properties.

One of the key results of the last section is Lemma 4.2, which observes that a matrix with (strong) $(\ell+1)$ -orthogonality also has addressable (strong) $\ell$ -orthogonality. Immediately, this leads us to the realisation that to construct a quantum code supporting addressable $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ gates, single-index inter-block $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates, or, most generally, single-index $U_{P}^{\beta}$ gates, where $\deg(P)=\ell$ , we need only construct matrices with $(\ell+1)$ -orthogonality, which in turn requires classical codes with the $(\ell+1)$ -multiplication property.

Since Reed-Solomon [RS60] and algebraic geometry codes [Gop82] naturally satisfy such multiplication properties, we are able to build a wide array of codes supporting these gates addressably. There is, however, one unfortunate feature of this, but we will be able to partially rectify it. In general, requiring a classical code to have the $\ell$ -multiplication property for larger $\ell$ worsens its parameters, which will in turn worsen the parameters of the resulting quantum code $\mathcal{Q}$ . In particular, we know that the $\ell$ -multiplication property on the classical code is enough to ensure transversality of gates such as $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ , $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ and $U_{P}^{\beta}$ , where $\deg(P)=\ell$ , but to obtain their (single-index) addressability, if we are going to use Lemma 4.2, we must require $(\ell+1)$ -multiplication of the classical code. This turns out to worsen the resulting parameters of the final quantum code by a factor of $\frac{\ell}{\ell+1}$ , which is particularly unfortunate for the most important case of $\ell=3$ . However, we are able to amend this issue in the case of Reed-Solomon codes. By appealing to the internal structure of these codes, we in fact show in Section 5.2 that a Reed-Solomon code with only $\ell$ multiplications can lead to a matrix with addressable strong $\ell$ -orthogonality (rather than $\ell-1$ ), so that in the case of Reed-Solomon codes, we may bypass Lemma 4.2. This improves the parameters of the resulting quantum codes supporting the above gates for Reed-Solomon codes, which could be an important difference given that Reed-Solomon-based constructions could turn out to have some practical importance.

By contrast, we are not able to show a similar result for algebraic geometry codes. In Section 5.3, we generalise the construction of [WHY24] to obtain algebraic geometry codes satisfying the $(\ell+1)$ -multiplication property which, via Lemma 4.2, will suffice to construct codes with addressable gates such as $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ , $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ and $U_{P}^{\beta}$ , where $\deg(P)=\ell$ . A result akin to what we achieve for Reed-Solomon codes, showing that an algebraic geometry code supporting only $\ell$ multiplications can be used to construct a matrix with addressable (strong) $\ell$ -orthogonality, would likely improve the parameters of the resulting quantum code supporting the stated addressable gates. Further investigation into this is left to future work. Accordingly, the best achievable parameters for a quantum code supporting addressable gates such as $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ , $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ and $U_{P}^{\beta}$ may be improvable in future.

Note that by using the qudit code-to-qubit code conversion methods of Section 6, all results obtained for codes on qudits (of dimension $2^{t}$ ) can be obtained for qubit codes, up to some loss in parameters. Note that, in certain places, if we claim improved parameters of a qudit quantum code, we are tacitly stating that the resultant qubit quantum code has improved parameters too, since converting the code to a qubit code via any given method would lead to improved parameters on the latter code as well. As usual, Reed-Solomon codes are only asymptotically good if one allows a growing field size, meaning the resulting qubit code will be not quite asymptotically good. By contrast, algebraic geometry codes are asymptotically good over a fixed finite field, leading also to asymptotically good codes over qubits.

It is interesting that the idea to obtain a matrix with addressable (strong) $\ell$ -orthogonality via a code with (strong) $(\ell+1)$ -multiplication is quite reminiscent of the folklore statement that a transversal gate in the $(\ell+1)$ -th level of the Clifford hierarchy implies a transversal and addessable gate in the $\ell$ -th level of the Clifford hierarchy; this folklore statement is discussed in Section 2.2. The reader may even wonder if these two observations are secretly the same thing. This is, however, not the case. Our observation that $(\ell+1)$ -multiplications leads to the addressability of these gates is strictly stronger, and can lead to considerable savings in parameters. For example, consider the $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ gate. As discussed in Appendix B, for all large enough fields $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , the smallest $\ell$ for which $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ is the second level of the Clifford hierarchy is $\ell=3$ , the smallest $\ell$ for which it is in the 3rd level is $\ell=7$ , the smallest to get into the 4th level is $\ell=15$ , and the smallest to get into the 5th level is $\ell=31$ . The values of $\ell$ required to get into successive levels of the Clifford hierarchy appear to be exponentially increasing, and we believe that further analysis may prove this to be true for all values of $\ell$ . The consequence is that, by using the given folklore statement, building codes with addressable $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ gates would incur far worse parameters than with our methods. Again, this is because building the classical code supporting $\ell$ -multiplications for larger $\ell$ gives worse parameters on the classical code, and resultantly on the quantum code also. If one were to use this folklore statement, it would seem that the number of multiplications required to support an addressable $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ gate in the $t$ -th level of the Clifford hierarchy is $\ell=2^{t+1}-1$ . On the other hand, our method requires only $\ell=2^{t}-1$ multiplications, which leads to an improvement in the final parameters of the quantum code by a factor of $\frac{2^{t+1}+1}{2^{t}+1}\approx 2$ . Our method of building codes with these addressable gates is therefore strictly stronger in this case, and we believe as the possibility of supporting more general diagonal Clifford hierarchy gates addressably opens up, it will in general be beneficial to consider our methods over the folklore result discussed in Section 2.2.

### 5.1 Multiplication Property for Classical Codes

Let us first discuss how we can obtain matrices $G$ with the (strong) $(\ell+1)$ -orthogonality property, which will give us addressable (strong) $\ell$ -orthogonality via Lemma 4.2. As observed in prior works [HH18, KT19, WHY24, Ngu24, GG24, NP24], such matrices can be constructed from classical codes with (strong) $(\ell+1)$ -multiplication property, which we now define.

#### Definition 5.1.

We say that $C$ has the $\ell$ -multiplication property with respect to $\sigma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{N}$ if, for all $c^{1},\dots,c^{\ell}\in C$ , it holds that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{i}c^{1}_{i}c^{2}_{i}\dots c^{\ell}_{i}=0. $$

We say that $C$ has the strong $\overline{\ell}$ -multiplication property with respect to $\sigma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{N}$ if, for all $\ell\leqslant\overline{\ell}$ , for all $c^{1},\ldots,c^{\ell}\in C$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{i}c^{1}_{i}c^{2}_{i}\dots c^{\ell}_{i}=0. $$

For convenience, we will say that $C$ has the (strong) $\ell$ -multiplication property if there exists some $0\neq\sigma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{N}$ for which the respective equations hold.

#### Remark 5.2.

In the situation that the code $C$ contains the all-ones vector, then the $\ell$ -multiplication property with respect to $\sigma$ implies the strong $\ell$ -multiplication property with respect to $\sigma$ .

Let us now show how classical codes with the (strong) multiplication properties can give rise to matrices with the (strong) orthogonality property, by puncturing their generator matrix.

#### Lemma 5.3.

Consider a code $C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{N}$ of dimension $m$ . Given $k<m$ , let $n=N-m$ . If $C$ has the strong $\overline{\ell}$ -multiplication property, for some $\overline{\ell}\geqslant 2$ , with respect to $\sigma$ , where $\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k}$ are not zero, then there is an $m\times n$ matrix $G$ with the strong $\overline{\ell}$ -orthogonality property with respect to $(\Gamma,\tau)$ , where $\Gamma=(\sigma_{i})_{i=k+1}^{N}$ and $\tau=(\sigma_{i})_{i=1}^{k}$ . The same statement holds for the regular (not strong) $\ell$ -multiplication property and the regular $\ell$ -orthogonality property.

#### Proof.

Following the construction of Section 2.4, we pick a generator matrix $\tilde{G}$ of $C$ of the form

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}I_{k}&G_{1}\\
0&G_{0}.\end{pmatrix} $$

by row operations. Taking

$$ \displaystyle G=\begin{pmatrix}G_{1}\\
G_{0}\end{pmatrix}, $$

let us check that this definition of $G$ satisfies the strong $\overline{\ell}$ -orthogonality property. Denoting the rows of $\tilde{G}$ by $\tilde{g}^{1},\dots,\tilde{g}^{m}$ , and the rows of $G$ by $g^{1},\dots,g^{m}$ , the fact that $C$ has the strong $\overline{\ell}$ -multiplication property, and that the rows of $\tilde{G}$ are codewords of $C$ , means that for all $\ell\leqslant\overline{\ell}$ and all $a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{\ell}\in[m]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{i}\tilde{g}_{i}^{a_{1}}\tilde{g}_{i}^{a_{2}}\ldots\tilde{g}_{i}^{a_{l}}=0, $$

for some $\sigma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{N}$ . Because the first $k$ columns of $\tilde{G}$ are of the form $\begin{pmatrix}I_{k}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$ , this can be rewritten as

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{a_{1}}\mathbbm{1}[1\leqslant a_{1}=a_{2}=\dots=a_{\ell}\leqslant k]+\sum_{i=k+1}^{N}\sigma_{i}\tilde{g}^{a_{1}}_{i}\tilde{g}^{a_{2}}_{i}\cdots\tilde{g}^{a_{\ell}}_{i}=0, $$

or

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{k+i}{g}^{a_{1}}_{i}{g}^{a_{2}}_{i}\cdots{g}^{a_{\ell}}_{i}=\begin{cases}\sigma_{a_{1}}&\text{ if $1\leqslant a_{1}=a_{2}=\dots=a_{\ell}\leqslant m$}\\
0&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

This latter manipulations assumes that the field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ has characteristic 2, although the result naturally generalises with the appropriate minus signs when that is not the case.

The proof for the regular (non-strong) case follows in the same way. ∎

### 5.2 Generalised Reed-Solomon Codes

As discussed in the introduction to Section 5, evaluation codes such as Reed-Solomon codes naturally satisfy (strong) $(\ell+1)$ -multiplication. This can give rise to matrices with the (strong) $(\ell+1)$ -orthogonality property via Lemma 5.3, which can give rise to matrices with the addressable strong $\ell$ -orthogonality property via Lemma 4.2. However, as mentioned, taking a Reed-Solomon code with $(\ell+1)$ multiplications rather than $\ell$ leads to a loss in the final parameters of the quantum code by a factor of $\frac{\ell}{\ell+1}$ , which we would like to avoid. In this section, by leveraging the internal structure of Reed-Solomon codes, we will show that we can avoid this loss of parameters, and directly obtain addressable strong $\ell$ -orthogonality, by requiring only $\ell$ multiplications in our Reed-Solomon code. Note that our construction bears some similarity to that of Section 3.

#### Theorem 5.4.

Fix any $\overline{\ell},m,N,k\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $n\coloneq N-k$ . Supposing that $m<1+n/\overline{\ell}$ and $k\leqslant m$ , and that $q\geqslant N$ for some prime power $q$ , we can construct an $m\times n$ matrix $G=\begin{pmatrix}G_{1}\\ G_{0}\end{pmatrix}$ with entries in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ such that

- 1. $G$ has addressable strong $\overline{\ell}$ -orthogonality with respect to $\tau=\mathbf{1}^{k}$ ;

- 2. $d(\mathcal{G})\geqslant n-m+1$ and $d(\mathcal{G}_{0}^{\perp})\geqslant m-k+1$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\bm{\alpha}$ be a collection of $N$ distinct points in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , consider the Reed-Solomon code $\RS_{N,m}(\bm{\alpha})$ . Since the code has dimension $m\geqslant k$ , we can take a generating matrix of the following form

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{G}=\begin{bmatrix}I_{k}&G_{1}\\
0&G_{0}\end{bmatrix}. $$

As before, each row of $\tilde{G}$ corresponds to a polynomial $\tilde{g}^{a}$ of degree less than $m$ . We may suppose that the columns of $\tilde{G}$ corresponds to evaluation points $\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{N}$ . From Fact 2.11, for any $A\in[k]$ , there exists vector $\Gamma^{A}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$ such that for all polynomials $f$ of degree less than $n$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle f(\alpha_{A})+\sum_{i=k+1}^{N}\Gamma^{A}_{i-k}f(\alpha_{i})=0. $$

As in equation (50), we take the coefficients of $f(\alpha_{A})$ to be 1 by normalizing the other coefficients. Given any $\ell\leqslant\overline{\ell}$ and any $a_{1},\ldots,a_{\ell}\in[m]$ , we have that $\tilde{g}^{a_{1}}\tilde{g}^{a_{2}}\ldots\tilde{g}^{a_{\ell}}$ is a polynomial of degree at most $\ell(m-1)\leqslant\overline{\ell}(m-1)<n$ . Thus, we may apply Equation (162), to find that

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\tilde{g}^{a_{1}}(\alpha_{A})\tilde{g}^{a_{2}}(\alpha_{A})\ldots\tilde{g}^{a_{\ell}}(\alpha_{A})+\sum_{i=k+1}^{N}\Gamma^{A}_{i-k}\tilde{g}^{a_{1}}(\alpha_{i})\tilde{g}^{a_{2}}(\alpha_{i})\ldots\tilde{g}^{a_{\ell}}(\alpha_{i}) \displaystyle=\mathbf{1}_{a_{1}=a_{2}=\ldots=a_{\ell}=A}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma^{A}_{i}\tilde{g}^{a_{1}}(\alpha_{i+k})\tilde{g}^{a_{2}}(\alpha_{i+k})\ldots\tilde{g}^{a_{\ell}}(\alpha_{i+k}). $$

Therefore,

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma_{i}^{A}g_{i}^{a_{1}}g_{i}^{a_{2}}\ldots g_{i}^{a_{\ell}}=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if }a_{1}=a_{2}=\ldots=a_{\ell}=A\\
0&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}. $$

We have shown that $G$ has the addressable strong $\overline{\ell}$ -orthogonality property with respect to the all-ones vector $\tau=\mathbf{1}^{k}$ .

Let $C$ denote the code with generator matrix $\tilde{G}$ , and let $T$ denote the first $k$ indices. As in the case of equation (45), we have $\mathcal{G}_{0}=C_{T=0}$ and $\mathcal{G}=C_{\setminus T}$ . By Lemma 2.7, Fact 2.8, as well as Theorems 2.12 and 2.13, we have $d(\mathcal{G})\geqslant d(C)-k=n-m+1$ and $d(\mathcal{G}_{0}^{\perp})\geqslant d(C^{\perp})-k=m-k+1$ . ∎

With this done, our framework will finally bear fruit in the form of the following Reed-Solomon based construction of qudit quantum codes supporting transversal, addressable single qudit gates like $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ and single-index addressable multi-qudit gates like $U_{P}^{\beta}$ . As discussed, this result gives better parameters than would have been achieved otherwise if one had either simply used the folklore that transversal $\mathsf{CCCZ}$ implies single-index addressable $\mathsf{CCZ}$ , or by simply using Lemma 4.2.

#### Theorem 5.5.

Let $\overline{\ell},m,n,k,q$ satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 5.4. Then there exists an $[[n,k,d]]_{q}$ quantum code $\mathcal{Q}$ with $d\geqslant\min(n-m+1,m-k+1)$ such that, for any $e,\ell\leqslant\overline{\ell}$ , $\mathcal{Q}$ supports single-index addressable, transversal implementations of all $e$ -variable, degree $\ell$ polynomial gates $U_{P}^{\beta}$ across $e$ code blocks. This includes single-index addressability of $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ , as well as addressability of single-qudit gates such as $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ .

Choosing $m=\left\lfloor n/\overline{\ell}\right\rfloor$ and $k=m/2$ , we see that $\mathcal{Q}$ may be chosen to be asymptotically good (over a growing qudit size) with rate and relative distance at least $1/(2\overline{\ell})$ .

#### Remark 5.6.

The surprising result here is that with Reed-Solomon codes, one may do as well when it comes to addressability as for mere transversality, at least when it comes to the class of gates we study, namely diagonal Clifford hierarchy gates with entries $\pm 1$ on the diagonal. Indeed, one can check that these parameters match the parameters obtained for the transversality of the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate in [KT19, GG24]. This is because we have used the interal structure of Reed-Solomon codes, in particular in Theorem 5.5, and have thus improved the final parameters by a factor of $\frac{\overline{\ell}+1}{\overline{\ell}}$ , as claimed, relative to what would have been achieved via either the use of Lemma 4.2, and by a potentiall much larger factor by using the folklore observation discussed in Section 2.2. As a key example, we note that if one is satisfied with a growing field size, then a single-index addressable $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate may be obtained with rate and relative distance at least $1/6$ .

#### Remark 5.7.

Note that these are the same parameters as were obtained for the full addressability result for qudits, Theorem 3.1, and indeed the constructions are very similar, the present results offers greater generality in the construction at the expense of worse addressability properties (single-index addressability rather than addressability).

### 5.3 Algebraic Geometry Codes

In this section, we describe how to use algebraic geometry codes to construct addressable strong $\ell$ -orthogonal matrices over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ for which the corresponding quantum code $\mathcal{Q}$ is asymptotically good. Moreover, unlike for the Reed-Solomon codes, the field over which they are defined, $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , will be fixed, and will not grow with the field size, which means that the qubit codes that result from the conversions of Section 6 are asymptotically good.

As mentioned, however, unlike for the Reed-Solomon codes, we will not be able to obtain addressability using the internal structure of the code. Here, we will simply obtain $\ell$ orthogonality (for any $\ell$ ), and then appeal to Lemma 4.2 to get matrices with addressable orthogonality. We will not make an attempt to optimise constants in this construction. We hope that future work, perhaps leveraging the internal structure of algebraic geometry codes, in a similar way to the previous section, will establish what parameters may be achieved for a quantum code supporting single-index addressable gates, such as the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates, on qubits, or on a field of fixed size.

We note that the body of the construction follows as a simple corollary of previous work. A general construction may be formulated for any algebraic function field with enough rational places as a simple extension of Section 5 of [WHY24]. On the other hand, here, to expedite the presentation, and because we make no attempt to optimise parameters, we simply appeal to the properties of particular function fields, in the same way as [Ngu24].

#### Theorem 5.8.

For any $\overline{\ell}\geqslant 2$ , there exists some fixed $q=2^{t}$ and an explicit family of $[N,m,d]_{q}$ classical codes with the strong $\overline{\ell}$ -multiplication property respect to the all-ones vector $\mathbf{1}^{N}$ . Moreover, letting $d^{\perp}$ be the distance of the dual code, we have $m,d,d^{\perp}=\Theta(N)$ , as well as $m-k,d-k,d^{\perp}-k=\Theta(N)$ .

#### Proof.

The regular $\overline{\ell}$ -multiplication property and the statement on the parameters follows as a simple generalisation of the argument of Theorem 3.6 of [Ngu24], which uses the results of [GS95, Sti09], in particular by making the necessary replacements $3\mapsto\overline{\ell}$ . Moreover, since the code contains the all-ones vector, the regular $\overline{\ell}$ -multiplication property implies the strong $\overline{\ell}$ -multiplication property, as observed in Remark 5.2. ∎

#### Corollary 5.9.

For any $\overline{\ell}\geqslant 2$ , there exists some fixed $q=2^{t}$ and a family of matrices $G$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ with the strong $\overline{\ell}$ -orthogonality property with respect to all-ones vectors for which the corresponding quantum codes are explicit and asymptotically good. The same matrices satisfy addressable strong $(\overline{\ell}-1)$ -orthogonality with respect to the all-ones vector.

#### Proof.

This follows from the construction of Section 2.4 as well as Lemmas 5.3 and 4.2. ∎

Corollary 5.9 may be used to instantiate any of the results of Section 4 to produce asymptotically good qubit codes with various addressable gates. As an example that is of particular interest to us, we have the following.

#### Theorem 5.10.

There exists some fixed $q=2^{t}$ and a family of asymptotically good quantum codes over qudits of dimension $q$ such that a logical three-qudit non-Clifford gate may be executed on fixed intra-block (pairwise disjoint) triples of logical qudits via a depth-one physical circuit of $U_{q,7}^{\beta}$ gates.

#### Proof.

This is an immediate application of the construction of this section to the construction of Section 4.4. ∎

## 6 Qubit Codes from Qudit Codes

In this section, we will prove the main results of this work by converting the qudit codes constructed in Sections 3 to 5 to qubit codes, while preserving the addressability of their gates, and incurring only a small loss in their parameters. In large parts we follow the qudit-qubit conversion methods in [Ngu24], with some alterations for our particular situation.1919 19 We note that the indepedent work [GG24] presents qudit-qubit conversion methods that may be viewed as a generalisation of those in [Ngu24]. We leave to further work whether those constructions can apply in this situation, which could lead to a improvement in the parameters of the qubit code obtained. Each logical/physical qudit will ultimately be embedded into a larger number of logical/physical qubits in such a way as to preserve the structure of the code that allows for gates to be implemented addressably and transversally in each case.

In general, there is a large amount of flexibility in these constructions, allowing one to build quantum codes with many different sets of addressable gates at different lengths with different implementation depths at the physical level for the addressable transversal gates. Any of the codes described in Sections 3 to 5 can be converted into qubit codes with similar addressability properties. However, to focus our attention, we will focus on achieving two things:

- 1. We will convert the qudit code of Section 3 into a qubit code with the same addressability properties. Namely, any three logical qubits in one, two or three code blocks may be acted on with the qubit $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate via a depth-one circuit of physical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates. Because the qudit codes were constructed from Reed-Solomon codes, and are therefore only asymptotically good with a growing field size, the resulting qubit codes with have parameters $\left[\left[n,\Omega\left(\frac{n}{\text{polylog}(n)}\right),\Omega\left(\frac{n}{\text{polylog}(n)}\right)\right]\right]_{2}$ . Note that generalisations may easily be made to the other gates discussed such as $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ .

- 2. We will convert the qudit codes of Theorem 5.10 to qubit codes with similar addressability properties. Namely, the resulting qubit code will have its logical qubits partitioned into sets of three. Each set of three may be addressed with a logical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate by acting with a depth-one circuit of physical $\mathsf{Z}$ , $\mathsf{CZ}$ and $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates. Again, generalisations may easily be made to other gates. While this addressability is much weaker than in Point 1, these qubit codes will be asymptotically good.

These two conversions will be made in the coming sections. The latter conversion shares many ideas with the former and so will be stated more briefly. Therefore, we recommend that the coming sections are read in order.

### 6.1 Near-Asymptotically Good Qubit Codes with Transversal and Addressable CCZ Gates

In this section, we will prove the main result of the paper, which is the following.

#### Theorem 6.1 (Restatement of Theorem 1.1).

There exists an explicit family of quantum CSS codes over qubits with parameters

$$ \left[\left[n,\Omega\left(\frac{n}{\text{polylog}(n)}\right),\Omega\left(\frac{n}{\text{polylog}(n)}\right)\right]\right]_{2} $$

supporting a transversal, addressable $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate. Specifically, any three logical qubits across one, two, or three blocks of the code may be addressed with the logical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate via a depth-one circuit of physical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates.

#### 6.1.1 Expanding Qudits into Qubits

Let $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ denote the original code constructed in Section 3 for qudits of dimension $q=2^{t}$ with the addressable $\mathsf{CCZ}_{q}^{\beta}$ gate and denote its parameters as $[[n_{0},k_{0},d_{0}]]_{q}$ , where $q=2^{t}=n_{0}^{2}$ , and $k_{0},d_{0}=\Theta(n_{0})$ . The procedure begins by using the construction of Lemma 2.5 to convert $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ into a qubit code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ . We will use notation as in that lemma, as well as notation used throughout Section 2.3. In particular, we fix a self-dual basis $\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=0}^{t-1}$ for $\mathbb{F}_{2^{t}}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ , and let $\mathcal{B}:\mathbb{F}_{2^{t}}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{t}$ be the associated decomposition map. Let us call a block of $t$ qubits on $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ which corresponds to a $q$ -dimensional qudit in $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ a $q$ -block. Note that we have logical $q$ -blocks and physical $q$ -blocks. As qudits are converted into qubits under this map, the $\mathsf{CCZ}_{q}^{\beta}$ gate on qudits becomes the unitary $V^{\beta}\coloneq\theta^{\otimes 3}\left(\mathsf{CCZ}^{\beta}_{q}\right)$ , acting on $3t$ qubits as

$$ \displaystyle V^{\beta}\ket{\mathcal{B}(\eta_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(\eta_{2})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(\eta_{3})} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\tr(\beta\eta_1\eta_2\eta_3)}\ket{\mathcal{B}(\eta_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(\eta_{2})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(\eta_{3})},\;\forall\eta_{1},\eta_{2},\eta_{3},\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}. $$

Therefore, if $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ is a qudit code on which logical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ is implemented by physical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates, then $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ is a qubit code on which logical $V$ gates acting on logical $q$ -blocks are implemented by physical $V$ gates acting on physical $q$ -blocks.

The key idea of [Ngu24] is to modify the physical and logical spaces of the code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ so that the qubit $V^{\beta}$ gates become products of qubit $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates. At the logical level, this is achieved through a hard-coding of $t-1$ of the $t$ logical qubits in a logical $q$ -block to $\ket{0}$ , and with an appropriate choice of $\beta$ , the action of $V^{\beta}$ will be shown to correspond to that of $\mathsf{CCZ}$ , as is desired. At the physical level, the qubits are further encoded into a code that allows us to create the action of the $V^{\beta}$ gate using a depth-one circuit of $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates. The code into which they are further encoded is created via multiplication-friendly embeddings, which we now introduce.

#### 6.1.2 Multiplication-Friendly Embeddings

#### Definition 6.2 (Definition 4.4 of [Ngu24]).

For a field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ with $q=2^{t}$ , a degree- $\ell$ multiplication friendly embedding (MFE) of $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ into $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}$ consists of a pair of functions $(\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2},\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q})$ and a collection of $r$ -element permutations $\pi_{1},\cdots,\pi_{\ell}$ such that

- 1. $\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}:\mathbb{F}_{q}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}$ is an injective $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -linear map, and $\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q}$ is a surjective $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -linear map;

- 2. For all $\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{\ell}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , we have $\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}\alpha_{i}=\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}\left[\pi_{1}(\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\alpha_{1}))\star\pi_{2}(\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\alpha_{2}))\star\cdots\star\pi_{\ell}(\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\alpha_{\ell}))\right].$ (168)

#### Lemma 6.3 (Lemma 4.5 of [Ngu24]).

For all $t$ , there exists a degree-3 MFE of $\mathbb{F}_{2^{t}}$ into $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}$ where $r=t^{3}$ .

The use of the following corollary will be evident by the end of the next section.

#### Corollary 6.4.

Given a degree- $\ell$ MFE with maps $\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2},\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}$ and permutations $\pi_{1},\cdots,\pi_{\ell}$ , we can construct another degree- $\ell$ MFE by setting $\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}^{\prime}(\gamma)=(\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\gamma),\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\gamma),\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\gamma),\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\gamma))$ and changing the other functions accordingly.

#### Proof.

We set $\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}^{\prime}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{4r}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q}$ as $\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}^{\prime}(u)=\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}(u_{1},\cdots,u_{r})$ , and we let $\pi_{i}^{\prime}$ be $\pi_{i}$ acting on 4 copies of the embedding independently. Equation (168) follows straightforwardly. ∎

#### 6.1.3 Logical and Physical Modifications to the Code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$

Let us now describe how exactly we modify the code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , which we note has parameters $[[n_{1}=n_{0}t,k_{1}=k_{0}t,d_{1}]]_{2}$ . As mentioned, there will be a step that modifies its “logical space”, and a step that modifies its “physical space”. It will become more clear what this means.

Starting with the logical modification, we may enumerate the logical $Z$ -operators of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ as $\{\overline{Z}_{b,j}\}$ for $b\in[k_{0}],j\in[t]$ , so that, for each $b$ , the operators $\overline{Z}_{b,1},\cdots,\overline{Z}_{b,t}$ are the logical $Z$ operators for the $b$ -th block of $t$ logical qubits.

#### Lemma 6.5.

For every $b\in[k_{0}]$ , let us add the $Z$ -operators $\overline{Z}_{b,2},\cdots,\overline{Z}_{b,t}$ into the $Z$ -stabilizers of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ to create the code $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ . In the terminology of quantum codes, we “gauge-fix” the last $t-1$ logical qubits in every block of $t$ logical qubits. Then

- 1. $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ has parameters $[[n_{2}=n_{1},k_{2}=k_{0},d_{2}\geqslant d_{1}]]_{2}$ ;

- 2. For every $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , suppose a physical circuit $C(\beta)$ acting on the physical qubits of a code state of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ implements a logical intra-block $V^{\beta}$ gate acting on logical $q$ -blocks $A,B,C\in[k_{0}]$ . In other words, suppose $\displaystyle\overline{V^{\beta}[A,B,C]}=C(\beta).$ (169) Then the physical circuit $C(\alpha_{1}^{-1})$ acting on a code state of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ implements a logical intra-block $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate on logical qubits $A,B,C$ of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ . Similar conclusions hold for logical inter-block $V$ gates.

#### Proof.

As mentioned, the described procedure simply hardcodes the last $t-1$ qubits of every logical $q$ -block of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ to $\ket{0}$ . The code distance does not decrease from such a procedure. Therefore, a logical $V$ gate defined as in equation (167) acting on three logical $q$ -blocks evaluates as, for every $b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle V^{\beta}\ket{b_{1},0,\cdots,0}\ket{b_{2},0,\cdots,0}\ket{b_{3},0,\cdots,0} \displaystyle=V^{\beta}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{1}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{2}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{3}\alpha_{1})} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\tr(\beta b_1\al_1b_2\al_1b_3\al_1)}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{1}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{2}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{3}\alpha_{1})} \displaystyle=(-1)^{b_{1}b_{2}b_{3}\tr(\beta\al_1\al_1\al_1)}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{1}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{2}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{3}\alpha_{1})}. $$

By setting $\beta=\alpha_{1}^{-1}$ , we see that

$$ \displaystyle V^{\alpha_{1}^{-1}}\ket{b_{1},0,\cdots,0}\ket{b_{2},0,\cdots,0}\ket{b_{3},0,\cdots,0} \displaystyle=(-1)^{b_{1}b_{2}b_{3}\tr( \al_1\al_1)}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{1}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{2}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{3}\alpha_{1})} \displaystyle=(-1)^{b_{1}b_{2}b_{3}}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{1}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{2}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{3}\alpha_{1})}, $$

where the final equality follows from the self-duality of our chosen basis. ∎

#### Remark 6.6.

Clearly, hardcoding this many logical qubits to $0$ is quite wasteful. It would be interesting to see if it is possible to recover more addressable logical qubits per logical qudit, for example as was done for transversality by using reverse multiplication friendly encodings in [Ngu24], or via quantum multiplication friendly codes [GG24]. Indeed, we note it is certainly possible to do this and retain a certain amount of addressability. However, whether it is possible to do this and retain full addressability of the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate, which is the primary aim of this work, is not clear.

We now modify the physical space of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ . The high level idea is simple: we will construct, using a multiplication-friendly embedding, a quantum code $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{out}}$ which encodes every $q$ -block of $t$ qubits into $r$ qubits such that a $V$ gate acting on three $q$ -blocks may be implemented by $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates acting on $3r$ qubits. The use of the multiplication-friendly embedding allows a larger number of bits to emulate the multiplication in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ via the star product.

Consider a degree-3 MFE as in Definition 6.2 with $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -linear maps $(\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2},\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q})$ and a collection of $r$ -element permutations $\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\pi_{3}$ . Recall that $\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}:\mathbb{F}_{q}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}$ is injective and $\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{q}$ is surjective. Let

$$ \displaystyle\phi=\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}\circ\mathcal{B}^{-1}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{t}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}, $$

which is an injective $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -linear map, and let $\mathcal{C}_{\text{out}}=\im(\phi)$ be a classical code. $\mathcal{C}_{\text{out}}$ may also be considered a quantum code $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{out}}$ with parameters $[[r,t,1]]_{2}$ via $\overline{\ket{u}}\coloneq\ket{\phi(u)}$ . From here, we have the following lemma.

#### Lemma 6.7.

Consider three standard basis states $\overline{\ket{u}}=\ket{\phi(u)}$ , $\overline{\ket{v}}=\ket{\phi(v)}$ , $\overline{\ket{w}}=\ket{\phi(w)}$ of $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{out}}$ for $u,v,w\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{t}$ . For all $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , the logical gate $V^{\beta}$ can be implemented by a depth-1 $\mathsf{CCZ}$ circuit.

#### Proof.

We are aiming to implement the logical gate $V^{\beta}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\overline{V^{\beta}\ket{u}\ket{v}\ket{w}} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\tr(\beta\B^{-1}(u)\B^{-1}(v)\B^{-1}(w))}\overline{\ket{u}}\overline{\ket{v}}\overline{\ket{w}}. $$

We emphasise that the overlines here indicate logical gates and states of the code $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{out}}$ . From equation (168), we see that

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}^{-1}(u)\mathcal{B}^{-1}(v)\mathcal{B}^{-1}(w) \displaystyle=\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}\left[\pi_{1}(\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\mathcal{B}^{-1}(u)))\star\pi_{2}(\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\mathcal{B}^{-1}(v)))\star\pi_{3}(\mathsf{ME}_{q\rightarrow 2}(\mathcal{B}^{-1}(w)))\right] \displaystyle=\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}\left[\pi_{1}(\phi(u))\star\pi_{2}(\phi(v))\star\pi_{3}(\phi(w))\right]. $$

Moreover, suppose $\beta=\sum_{i\in[t]}b_{i}\alpha_{i}$ , let $\vec{b}=(b_{1},\cdots,b_{t})$ . Then for all $\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , since $\{\alpha_{i}\}$ is a self-dual basis we have $\tr[\beta\gamma]=\vec{b}\cdot\mathcal{B}(\gamma)$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\tr(\beta\B^{-1}(u)\B^{-1}(v)\B^{-1}(w)) \displaystyle=\vec{b}\cdot\left(\mathcal{B}(\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}\left[\pi_{1}(\phi(u))\star\pi_{2}(\phi(v))\star\pi_{3}(\phi(w))\right])\right). $$

Note that $\mathcal{B}\circ\mathsf{ME}_{2\rightarrow q}:\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{2}^{t}$ is a surjective $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -linear function. Let $T$ be the matrix representation of this function, and let $\Lambda(\beta)=\vec{b}T\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}$ where $\vec{b}$ is considered a row vector and $\vec{b}T$ is simply matrix multiplication. Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\tr(\beta\B^{-1}(u)\B^{-1}(v)\B^{-1}(w)) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\Lambda(\beta)_{j}\left[\pi_{1}(\phi(u))\star\pi_{2}(\phi(v))\star\pi_{3}(\phi(w))\right]_{j} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\Lambda(\beta)_{j}\pi_{1}(\phi(u))_{j}\pi_{2}(\phi(v))_{j}\pi_{3}(\phi(w))_{j} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\Lambda(\beta)_{j}\phi(u)_{\pi_{1}^{-1}(j)}\phi(v)_{\pi_{2}^{-1}(j)}\phi(w)_{\pi_{3}^{-1}(j)}. $$

We can create this phase with a depth-1 $\mathsf{CCZ}$ circuit, namely

$$ \displaystyle\overline{V^{\beta}\ket{u}\ket{v}\ket{w}} \displaystyle=\bigotimes_{j=1}^{r}\mathsf{CCZ}^{\Lambda(\beta)_{j}}[\pi_{1}^{-1}(j),\pi_{2}^{-1}(j),\pi_{3}^{-1}(j)]\ket{\phi(u)}\ket{\phi(v)}\ket{\phi(w)}. $$

Since $\Lambda(\beta)_{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}$ , $\mathsf{CCZ}^{\Lambda(\beta)_{j}}$ is simply $\mathsf{CCZ}$ if $\Lambda(\beta)_{j}=1$ and identity otherwise. This circuit has depth-1 since $\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\pi_{3}$ are permutations. ∎

#### Corollary 6.8.

Using the duplicated MFE as in Corollary 6.4, a depth-4 logical circuit of $V$ gates acting on code states of $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{out}}$ can be implemented by a depth-1 $\mathsf{CCZ}$ physical circuit.

#### Proof.

We construct the encoding function $\phi$ as in equation (175), and take the classical code $\mathcal{C}_{\text{out}}$ , which again may be viewed as a quantum code $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{out}}$ . Following the same proof as above, the four $V$ gates acting on any $q$ -block can each be implemented with a collection of non-overlapping CCZ circuit acting on $r$ of the $4r$ qubits of the encoded block. Therefore, we can arrange them all into a depth-1 $\mathsf{CCZ}$ circuit. ∎

We can now in a position to prove Theorem 6.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 6.1.

Let $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ be the qudit CSS code from Theorem 3.1 with parameters $[[n_{0},k_{0},d_{0}]]_{q}$ . We know that $k_{0},d_{0}=\Theta(n_{0})$ , where $q=2^{t}=n_{0}^{2}$ . Applying Lemma 2.5, we get a qubit CSS code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ with parameters $[[n_{1}=n_{0}t,k_{1}=k_{0}t,d_{1}\geqslant d_{0}]]_{2}$ . $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ supports a depth-4 implementation of addressable intra-block $V$ gates, and a depth-1 implementation of addressable inter-block $V$ gates.

Next we apply Lemma 6.5 to get a qubit CSS code $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ with parameters $[[n_{2}=n_{0}t,k_{2}=k_{0},d_{2}\geqslant d_{0}]]_{2}$ . On $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ , the logical actions of $V$ gates are translated into $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates, which means addressable intra-block $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates and inter-block $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates are implemented by circuits of $V$ gates of depth four and depth one, respectively.

Finally, if we want addressable inter-block $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates to be implemented by a depth-1 $\mathsf{CCZ}$ circuit, we can encode every physical $q$ -block of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ into a $[[t^{3},t,1]]_{2}$ quantum code $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{out}}$ constructed from the degree-3 MFE in Lemma 6.3. The resulting qubit CSS code $\mathcal{Q}_{3}$ has parameters $[[n_{3}=n_{0}t^{3},k_{2}=k_{0},d_{3}\geqslant d_{0}]]_{2}$ . The transversal implementation of addressable inter-block $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates is guaranteed by Lemma 6.7. If we additionally want addressable intra-block $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates to be implemented by a depth-1 $\mathsf{CCZ}$ circuit, we concatenate using the code $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{out}}$ in Corollary 6.8 instead and obtain the resulting qubit code $\mathcal{Q}_{3}^{\prime}$ with parameters $[[n_{3}=4n_{0}t^{3},k_{2}=k_{0},d_{3}\geqslant d_{0}]]_{2}$ . Since $t=2\log n_{0}$ , we obtain the desired result. ∎

#### Remark 6.9.

Being able to execute the intra-block $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates via a depth one circuit comes at the expense of a longer code. As is clear from Corollary 6.8, and as we mention in the proof, one could instead obtain a shorter code at the expense of greater implementation depth. Now, as stated in Remark 3.4, the construction is generalisable to higher-degree polynomial gates such as $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ .2020 20 This is possible because, for example, the argument of Lemma 4.5 of [Ngu24] can be easily generalised to obtain higher degree MFEs. In particular, there exists an explicit degree- $\ell$ MFE of $\mathbb{F}_{2^{t}}$ into $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}$ for which $r=t^{\ell}$ . It is also possible to use the quantum multiplication friendly codes of [GG24]. In this case, the greater depth needed for the intra-block implementation could again be traded off into a longer code length, if desired.

One can even take these thoughts a step further and note that if Lemma 6.7 (and Corollary 6.8) were not applied, then the logical, addressable $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate would be implementable by a circuit of physical $V^{\beta}$ gates, implying a much shorter code, but with a higher (but still low) implementation depth. Indeed, the $V^{\beta}$ gates would be implementable by a circuit of $\mathsf{Z},\mathsf{CZ}$ and $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates.2121 21 This is true because $V^{\beta}=\theta^{\otimes 3}(\mathsf{CCZ}_{q}^{\beta})$ must be a diagonal gate in exactly the third level of the Clifford hierarchy with $\pm 1$ on the diagonal. A diagonal gate with entries $\pm 1$ on the diagonal must be implementable via a circuit of $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates [HZSA14], and so the fact that $V^{\beta}$ can be implemented by a circuit of (qubit) $\mathsf{Z}$ , $\mathsf{CZ}$ and $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates follows from the fact that $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates are independent (meaning no non-trivial combination of them acts identically), and $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ is in exactly the $\ell$ -th level of the Clifford hierarchy.

### 6.2 Asymptotically Good Qubit Codes with Transversal and Addressable CCZ Gates on Pre-Designed Intrablock Triples

In this section, we will prove the second main result of the paper, which is the following.

#### Theorem 6.10 (Restatement of Theorem 1.2).

There exists an explicit family of quantum CSS codes over qubits with parameters

$$ \left[\left[n,\Theta(n),\Theta(n)\right]\right]_{2}, $$

meaning that it is asymptotically good, supporting a transversal, addressable $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate on pre-designed (pairwise disjoint) intra-block triples of logical qubits. Specifically, the logical qubits in one block of the code are partitioned into sets of three, and one may address any such set with the $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate via a depth-one circuit of physical $\mathsf{Z}$ , $\mathsf{CZ}$ and $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates.

The steps taken in this section are similar at a high level to those of Section 6.1, with certain differences at a lower level. We denote by $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ the qudit codes of Theorem 5.10, writing their parameters as $[[n_{0},3k_{0},d_{0}]]_{q}$ , where $q=2^{t}$ is fixed, and $k_{0},d_{0}=\Theta(n_{0})$ . We note that the code $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ has $k_{0}$ sets of 3 logical qudits. Applying once more the construction of Lemma 2.5, we obtain a code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ with parameters $[[n_{0}t,3k_{0}t,d_{1}\geqslant d_{0}]]_{2}$ . This is done, as usual, via a self-dual basis $\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=0}^{t-1}$ for $\mathbb{F}_{2^{t}}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ , and with the decomposition map $\mathcal{B}:\mathbb{F}_{2^{t}}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}^{t}$ . Recall that in the code $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ , it was possible to address any of the $k_{0}$ sets of 3 logical qudits with the gate $W^{\beta}$ via a depth-one circuit of physical $U_{7}^{\gamma}$ gates, where

$$ W^{\beta}\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\ket{\eta_{3}}=\exp\left(i\pi\tr\left(\beta\sum_{\{a,b,c\}\in\{1,2,3\}}\eta_{a}^{4}\eta_{b}^{2}\eta_{c}\right)\right)\ket{\eta_{1}}\ket{\eta_{2}}\ket{\eta_{3}}. $$

Under the embedding into qubits, these gates become a $3t$ -qubit, and a $t$ -qubit gate, respectively, which we denote

$$ \displaystyle\Pi^{\beta} \displaystyle\coloneq\theta^{\otimes 3}(W^{\beta}) \displaystyle\Sigma^{\gamma} \displaystyle\coloneq\theta(U_{7}^{\gamma}). $$

The $k_{0}$ sets of 3 logical qudits in $\mathcal{Q}_{0}$ become $k_{0}$ sets of 3 logical $q$ -blocks in $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ . Then, in the code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , a physical circuit of $\Sigma$ gates acting transversally on the physical $q$ -blocks executes a logical $\Pi^{\beta}$ gate between one of these sets of three logical $q$ -blocks; one may address any set of three logical $q$ -blocks with the logical $\Pi^{\beta}$ gate. Enumerating these sets of three $q$ -blocks in $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ by $A\in[k_{0}]$ , let $\overline{\Pi^{\beta}[A]}$ denote the logical $\Pi^{\beta}$ gate acting on the $A$ -th set of 3 logical $q$ -blocks. In the same way as last time, it is convenient to write

$$ \overline{\Pi^{\beta}[A]}=C(\beta), $$

where $C(\beta)$ is the physical circuit of $\Sigma$ gates executing $\Pi^{\beta}$ gate on the $A$ -th set of three logical $q$ -blocks. Again in a similar way to last time, we will now hardcode $t-1$ of the $t$ qubits in each logical $q$ -block to $\ket{0}$ to create a code $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ with parameters $[[n_{0}t,3k_{0},d_{2}\geqslant d_{0}]]_{2}$ . However, this time, the hardcoding will go slightly differently. Given any set of three logical $q$ -blocks labelled by $A\in[k_{0}]$ , in the first of these $q$ -blocks we hardcode all but the first logical qubit to $\ket{0}$ , whereas in the second logical $q$ -block we hardcode all but the second logical qubit to $\ket{0}$ , and finally in the third logical $q$ -block we hardcode all but the third logical qubit to $\ket{0}$ . The gate $\Pi^{\beta}$ acts on such a set of three $q$ -blocks as

$$ \displaystyle\Pi^{\beta} \displaystyle\ket{b_{1},0,0,\ldots,0}\ket{0,b_{2},0,\ldots,0}\ket{0,0,b_{3},\ldots,0}=\Pi^{\beta}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{1}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{2}\alpha_{2})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{3}\alpha_{3})} \displaystyle=\exp\left(i\pi\tr\left(\beta\sum_{\{a,b,c\}\in\{1,2,3\}}(b_{a}\alpha_{a})^{4}(b_{b}\alpha_{b})^{2}(b_{c}\alpha_{c})\right)\right)\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{1}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{2}\alpha_{2})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{3}\alpha_{3})} \displaystyle=\exp\left(i\pi b_{1}b_{2}b_{3}\tr\left(\beta\sum_{\{a,b,c\}\in\{1,2,3\}}\alpha_{a}^{4}\alpha_{b}^{2}\alpha_{c}\right)\right)\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{1}\alpha_{1})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{2}\alpha_{2})}\ket{\mathcal{B}(b_{3}\alpha_{3})}, $$

where going into the third line we have used the fact that $x^{2}=x$ for any $x\in\mathbb{F}_{2}$ and that $\tr$ is an $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -linear function. Given that we ultimately wish to execute the logical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate, for which we want the phase $(-1)^{b_{1}b_{2}b_{3}}$ , we define $\hat{\beta}$ to be any element of $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ satisfying

$$ \tr\left(\hat{\beta}\sum_{\{a,b,c\}\in\{1,2,3\}}\alpha_{a}^{4}\alpha_{b}^{2}\alpha_{c}\right)=1. $$

Note that a hard-coded logical $q$ -block encodes exactly one logical qubit. Then, on a set of three hardcoded logical $q$ -blocks, the logical gate $\Pi^{\hat{\beta}}$ acts as a (qubit) $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gate on the encoded logical qubits.

Having modified the logical space of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ to obtain the code $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ , it remains to modify the physical space. We want to be able to enact the gate $\Sigma^{\gamma}$ on physical $q$ -blocks of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ via a depth-one circuit of $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates, for $\ell\leqslant 3$ . The action of the gate $\Sigma^{\gamma}$ is as follows. With $u\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{t}$ , we note that $\mathcal{B}^{-1}(u)=\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}=u_{i}\alpha_{i}$ , and

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{\gamma}\ket{u} \displaystyle=\exp\left[i\pi\tr(\gamma(\mathcal{B}^{-1}(u))^7)\right]\ket{u} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\left(\mathcal{B}^{-1}(u)\right)^{7}=\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}u_{i}\alpha_{i}^{7} \displaystyle+\sum_{i<j}u_{i}u_{j}\left(\alpha_{i}^{6}\alpha_{j}+\alpha_{i}^{5}\alpha_{j}^{2}+\alpha_{i}^{4}\alpha_{j}^{3}+\alpha_{i}^{3}\alpha_{j}^{4}+\alpha_{i}^{2}\alpha_{j}^{5}+\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}^{6}\right) \displaystyle+\sum_{i<j<k}u_{i}u_{j}u_{k}\left(\alpha_{i}^{4}\alpha_{j}^{2}\alpha_{k}+\alpha_{i}^{4}\alpha_{j}\alpha_{k}^{2}+\alpha_{i}^{2}\alpha_{j}^{4}\alpha_{k}+\alpha_{i}^{2}\alpha_{j}\alpha_{k}^{4}+\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}^{4}\alpha_{k}^{2}+\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}^{2}\alpha_{k}^{4}\right) $$

where we have used the same formula as in Equations (135) and (136), albeit slightly re-written. Therefore, the desired phase is

$$ \exp\left[i\pi\tr(\gamma(\mathcal{B}^{-1}(u))^7)\right]=\exp\left[i\pi\left(\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}u_{i}\kappa_{i}+\sum_{i<j}u_{i}u_{j}\kappa_{ij}+\sum_{i<j<k}u_{i}u_{j}u_{k}\kappa_{ijk}\right)\right], $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{i} \displaystyle=\tr\left(\gamma\alpha_{i}^{7}\right) \displaystyle\kappa_{ij} \displaystyle=\tr\left[\gamma\left(\alpha_{i}^{6}\alpha_{j}+\alpha_{i}^{5}\alpha_{j}^{2}+\alpha_{i}^{4}\alpha_{j}^{3}+\alpha_{i}^{3}\alpha_{j}^{4}+\alpha_{i}^{2}\alpha_{j}^{5}+\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}^{6}\right)\right] \displaystyle\kappa_{ijk} \displaystyle=\tr\left[\gamma\left(\alpha_{i}^{4}\alpha_{j}^{2}\alpha_{k}+\alpha_{i}^{4}\alpha_{j}\alpha_{k}^{2}+\alpha_{i}^{2}\alpha_{j}^{4}\alpha_{k}+\alpha_{i}^{2}\alpha_{j}\alpha_{k}^{4}+\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}^{4}\alpha_{k}^{2}+\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}^{2}\alpha_{k}^{4}\right)\right]. $$

One could, therefore, enact the gate $\Sigma^{\gamma}$ on a physical $q$ -block of qubits of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ via the circuit

$$ \prod_{i=0}^{t-1}\mathsf{Z}^{\kappa_{i}}[i]\;\prod_{i<j}\mathsf{CZ}^{\kappa_{ij}}[i,j]\;\prod_{i<j<k}\mathsf{CCZ}^{\kappa_{ijk}}[i,j,k] $$

which is a non-transversal circuit of qubits $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates with $\ell\leqslant 3$ . However, we wish to obtain a depth-one circuit of $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates. To obtain this, it is sufficient to simply modify the physical space of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ by duplicating each physical qubit $\Omega$ times,2323 23 This simply means further encoding each physical qubit of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ into the code given by $\ket{0}\mapsto\ket{0}^{\otimes\Omega}$ ; $\ket{1}\mapsto\ket{1}^{\otimes\Omega}$ . where $\Omega$ is the maximum number of times a qubit is involved in the circuit in Equation (200); indeed one can always choose $\Omega=1+(t-1)+\begin{pmatrix}t-1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}=1+\frac{t(t-1)}{2}$ . Then, these qubits may be acted on with a depth-one circuit of physical $\mathsf{Z},\mathsf{CZ}$ and $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates to create the desired phase $\exp\left[i\pi\tr\left(\gamma(\mathcal{B}^{-1}(u))^{7}\right)\right]$ . From here, we may prove Theorem 6.10.

#### Proof of Theorem 6.10.

The proof follows in essentially the same way as the proof of Theorem 6.1. In this case, the code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ has parameters $[[n_{0}t,3k_{0}t,d_{1}\geqslant d_{0}]]_{2}$ , and so the code $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ has parameters $[[n_{0}t,3k_{0},d_{2}\geqslant d_{0}]]_{2}$ . After the duplication of each physical qubit $\Omega$ times, one obtains the final code $\mathcal{Q}_{3}$ with parameters $[[n_{0}t\Omega,3k_{0},d_{3}\geqslant d_{0}]]_{2}$ . Since $t$ , and therefore $\Omega$ , are constants, this code is asymptotically good, and the $k_{0}$ sets of 3 logical qubits may be addressed with logical $\mathsf{CCZ}$ gates in the way described by construction. ∎

#### Remark 6.11.

Note that the modification of the physical space here by duplicating qubits is morally the same as the use of the MFEs in Section 6.1, although it is phrased differently here for convenience.

## Appendix A Addressable $T$ Gates via Addressable Triorthogonality

In this section, we prove that a binary matrix with the addressable 3-orthogonality property, as defined in Section 4.1, leads to a quantum code with an addressable $T$ gate, up to the action of a corrective Clifford. While we do not have an instantiation in mind, this directly extends the original notion of triorthogonal matrices/triorthogonal quantum codes defined by Bravyi and Haah [BH12] (which coincides exactly with our definition of 3-orthogonality for a binary matrix) for which the associated quantum code can support a transversal $T$ -gate, up to a corrective Clifford. Accordingly, we name the matrices, and the corresponding quantum codes “addressable triorthogonal”. Although this is just our definition of addressable 3-orthogonality for a binary matrix, we enunciate this here.

#### Definition A.1.

A matrix $G\in(\mathbb{F}_{2})^{m\times n}$ with rows $(g^{a})_{a=1}^{m}$ is called addressable triorthogonal if, for some $k\in[m]$ , for every $A\in[k]$ , there exists a vector $\Gamma^{A}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ such that, for all $a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\in[m]$ ,

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma_{i}^{A}g_{i}^{a_{1}}g_{i}^{a_{2}}g_{i}^{a_{3}}=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if }a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=A\\
0&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}. $$

One can check that this definition exactly coincides with the notion of addressable 3-orthogonality for a binary matrix given in Section 4.1. We also note that, given Lemma 4.2, a natural way to obtain addressable triorthogonal matrices is via the construction of binary matrices with 4-orthogonality, also defined in Section 4.1. We now show the claim that the quantum code $\mathcal{Q}$ associated to a addressable triorthogonal matrix can support an addressable $T$ gate, up to corrective Clifford operations.

#### Theorem A.2.

Suppose $G$ is an addressable triorthogonal matrix. Then, the following is true when acting on a code state of the associated quantum code $\mathcal{Q}$ , defined in Equation (78):

$$ \overline{T[A]}=U_{A}T^{\Gamma^{A}}, $$

for some Clifford operation $U_{A}$ .

#### Proof.

Our proof closely follows that of Lemma 2 in [BH12]. As throughout the paper, arithmetic takes place in the finite field (the binary field in this case), unless we specify otherwise.

Given $u\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}$ , the logical computational basis state $\overline{\ket{u}}$ in the quantum code $\mathcal{Q}$ is

$$ \overline{\ket{u}}\propto\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{0}}\Ket{\sum_{a=1}^{k}u_{a}g^{a}+g}, $$

and we aim to show that there is a Clifford operation $U_{A}$ such that

$$ U_{A}T^{\Gamma^{A}}\overline{\ket{u}}=\exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{4}u_{A}\right)\overline{\ket{u}}. $$

We first consider some state $\ket{f}$ , where $f=\sum_{a=1}^{m}u_{a}g^{a}$ , for some $u_{a}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}$ . Then,

$$ T^{\Gamma^{A}}\ket{f}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{4}\Gamma_{i}^{A}f_{i}\right)\ket{f}. $$

We then use the fact from the proof of Lemma 2 of [BH12] that, for a binary vector $y\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m}$ ,

$$ \exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{4}\sum_{a=1}^{m}y_{a}\right)=\exp\underbrace{\left(\frac{i\pi}{4}\sum_{a=1}^{m}y_{a}-\frac{i\pi}{2}\sum_{a<b}y_{a}y_{b}+i\pi\sum_{a<b<c}y_{a}y_{b}y_{c}\right)}_{\text{Literal sums of integers}}, $$

where, here, sums on the right-hand side are the usual sums of integers, but we emphasise that the sum on the left-hand side takes place in the field $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ (it is taken modulo 2), as usual.

Now, referring to the definition of addressable triorthogonality, we see that there are integers $\Lambda_{a}^{A}$ , for $a\in[m]$ , and $\Lambda_{ab}^{A}$ for $a,b\in[m]$ , $a<b$ , depending only on the matrix and the choice of $A\in[k]$ , for which

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma_{i}^{A}g_{i}^{a} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}2\Lambda_{A}^{A}+1&\text{ if }a=A,\\
2\Lambda_{a}^{A}&\text{ if }a\neq A,\end{cases} \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma_{i}^{A}g_{i}^{a}g_{i}^{b} \displaystyle=2\Lambda_{ab}^{A}, $$

where these sums are literal sums of integers. Note that Equation (207) is seen to be true by setting $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}$ in Definition A.1, whereas Equation (208) is seen to be true by taking $a_{1}\neq a_{2}=a_{3}$ . Therefore, Equations (205) to (208) and Definition A.1 give

$$ T^{\Gamma^{A}}\ket{f}=\exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{4}u_{A}\right)\prod_{a=1}^{m}\exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{2}u_{a}\Lambda^{A}_{a}\right)\prod_{a<b}\exp\left(i\pi\Lambda^{A}_{ab}u_{a}u_{b}\right)\ket{f}. $$

Note that the phase $\exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{4}u_{A}\right)$ is the phase that we want, whereas the remainder is the phase that we wish to cancel with a Clifford operation $U_{A}$ .

Now, by assumption our matrix $G$ is addressable 3-orthogonal with respect to the all-1’s vector, $\mathbf{1}^{k}$ .2424 24 Strictly speaking, this remark is redundant since the fact that $\tau\in(\mathbb{F}_{2}^{*})^{k}$ implies that $\tau=\mathbf{1}^{k}$ . Therefore, $G$ is 3-orthogonal with respect to $(\Gamma,\mathbf{1}^{k})$ , for some $\Gamma$ , by Lemma 4.1. Then, by Lemma 4.5, Assumption 2.9 is satisfied, meaning that the only linear dependence amongst the rows of $G$ is amongst the rows of $G_{0}$ which, as usual, is the latter $m-k$ rows of $G$ . Moreover, we may say without loss of generality that the rows of $G_{0}$ are linearly independent as well, since eliminating rows of $G_{0}$ does not alter the code $\mathcal{Q}$ . As such, $f_{i}=\sum_{a=1}^{m}u_{a}g^{a}_{i}$ implies that $(u_{a})_{a=1}^{m}$ are uniquely determined by $(f_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ , and so there exists a matrix $B\in(\mathbb{F}_{2})^{m\times n}$ such that $u_{a}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}B_{ai}f_{i}$ . Using the fact that

$$ \exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}\right)=\exp\underbrace{\left(\frac{i\pi}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}+i\pi\sum_{i<j}v_{i}v_{j}\right)}_{\text{Literal sums of integers}}, $$

for a binary vector $v\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ , one may check that the un-wanted phase may be written

$$ \prod_{a=1}^{m}\exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{2}u_{a}\Lambda^{A}_{a}\right)\prod_{a<b}\exp\left(i\pi\Lambda_{ab}^{A}u_{a}u_{b}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{2}\kappa_{i}f_{i}\right)\prod_{i<j}\exp\left(i\pi\kappa_{ij}f_{i}f_{j}\right), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{i} \displaystyle=\sum_{a=1}^{m}B_{ai}\Lambda_{a}^{A}+2\sum_{a<b}\Lambda^{A}_{ab}B_{ai}B_{bi} \displaystyle\kappa_{ij} \displaystyle=\sum_{a=1}^{m}B_{ai}B_{bj}\Lambda_{a}^{A}+\sum_{a<b}\Lambda_{ab}^{A}(B_{ai}B_{bj}+B_{aj}B_{bi}). $$

We therefore define the $n$ -qubit Clifford operator

$$ U_{A}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(S^{\dagger}[i])^{\kappa_{i}}\prod_{i<j}(\mathsf{CZ}[i,j])^{\kappa_{ij}}, $$

and we find that

$$ U_{A}T^{\Gamma^{A}}\ket{f}=\exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{4}u_{A}\right)\ket{f}. $$

Finally, referring back to the form of the logical computational basis state $\overline{\ket{u}}$ , we find by linearity that

$$ U_{A}T^{\Gamma^{A}}\overline{\ket{u}}=\exp\left(\frac{i\pi}{4}u_{A}\right)\overline{\ket{u}}, $$

as required. ∎

## Appendix B Diagonal Clifford Hierarchy for Qudits of Prime Power Dimension

In this section, we will discuss the importance of the following gates defined in Section 2.2 in the context of the Clifford hierarchy, which is a very important mathematical structure in fault-tolerant quantum computing:

$$ \displaystyle U_{q,P}=\sum_{\bm{\eta}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{e}}\exp(i\pi\tr(P(\boldsymbol{\eta})))\ket{\bm{\eta}}\bra{\bm{\eta}}. $$

These are diagonal gates defined for $e$ qudits of dimension $q=2^{t}$ , where $P$ is an $e$ -variate polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ . Our main intention here is to convince the reader that this set of gates not only appears as a straightforward generalisation of the well-known $\mathsf{C^{(\ell-1)}Z}$ gates, but is very natural in its own right.

While determining the full structure of the Clifford hierarchy is still an open problem, [CGK17] gave a full characterisation of the diagonal Clifford hierarchy gates for qudits of prime dimension. In particular, for a set of $n$ qubits, it was found that any such gate may be generated from gates of the form

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}}\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{2^{m}}P(j_{1},\ldots,j_{n})\right)\ket{\mathbf{j}}\bra{\mathbf{j}}, $$

where $P$ is an $n$ -variate polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ . The level in the Clifford hierarchy of the generated gate depends in a way made explicit in [CGK17] on the degree of the various polynomials $P$ and the “precisions” $m$ that appear. The same paper also observes, given the natural isomorphism between the states and gates of qudits of prime dimension (see Section 2.3), and a smaller number of qudits of prime-power dimension, and the associated isomorphism of Clifford hierarchies [Got24], that a similar statement must apply to the diagonal Clifford hierarchy for qudits of prime-power dimension. Indeed, it is easily shown that all such gates for $e$ qudits of dimension $q=2^{t}$ may be generated from gates of the form

$$ \sum_{\bm{\eta}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{e}}\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{2^{m}}\tr(P(\eta_1, \ldots, \eta_e))\right)\ket{\bm{\eta}}\bra{\bm{\eta}}. $$

The argument goes as follows. Because of the natural isomorphism, [CGK17] establishes for us that all diagonal entries must be some power of a phase $\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{2^{m}}\right)$ , and so the gate may be written as

$$ \sum_{\bm{\eta}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{e}}\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{2^{m}}\Theta(\bm{\eta})\right)\ket{\bm{\eta}}\bra{\bm{\eta}} $$

for some map $\Theta:\mathbb{F}_{q}^{e}\to\mathbb{Z}_{2^{m}}$ . Such a map may be written as $\Theta=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}2^{i}\theta_{i}$ , where $\theta_{i}:\mathbb{F}_{q}^{e}\to\mathbb{Z}_{2}=\mathbb{F}_{2}$ is some other map. Therefore, the gate (220) may be generated from gates of the form

$$ \sum_{\bm{\eta}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{e}}\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{2^{m}}\theta(\bm{\eta})\right)\ket{\bm{\eta}}\bra{\bm{\eta}} $$

where $\theta:\mathbb{F}_{q}^{e}\to\mathbb{F}_{2}$ is some map. However, we know that any map $\tilde{\theta}:\mathbb{F}_{q}^{e}\to\mathbb{F}_{q}$ may be written as some polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ via, for example, Lagrange interpolation. Therefore, since $\ker(\tr_{\mathbb{F}_{q}/\mathbb{F}_{2}})$ is a proper subset of $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , $\theta$ may be written as the trace of some polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ .

In particular, we find that gates $U_{q,P}$ are actually complete for the set of diagonal Clifford hierarchy gates with entries $\pm 1$ , and so they are certainly important to consider.

We would note, however, that whereas [CGK17] gives an explicit, and relatively simple description of the level of the Clifford hierarchy of any diagonal gate in terms of the degrees of its polynomials, our argument does not preserve this simple description. In fact, it seems that any description must necessarily be not so simple. For example, a natural generating set for the set of diagonal Clifford hierarchy gates with $\pm 1$ on the diagonal for one qudit of dimension $q$ are the gates $U_{q,\ell}^{\beta}$ defined in Section 2.2 as

$$ U_{q,\ell}^{\beta}=\sum_{\eta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}}\exp\left(i\pi\tr(\beta\eta^\ell)\right)\ket{\eta}\bra{\eta}. $$

Then, for small values of $\ell$ , one can check that the Clifford hierarchy level of $U_{q,\ell}^{\beta}$ behaves erratically with increasing $\ell$ , as opposed to the case of prime-dimensional qudits [CGK17], where the level of the Clifford hierarchy increases steadily with the polynomial degree. For example, one can check that (for all $q$ large enough) the smallest $\ell$ for which $U_{\ell}^{\beta}$ is in the 2nd level of the Clifford hierarchy is $\ell=3$ , the smallest $\ell$ for which $U_{q,\ell}^{\beta}$ is in the 3rd level of the Clifford hierarchy is $\ell=7$ , the smallest 4th level gate has $\ell=15$ , the smallest 5th level gate has $\ell=31$ , and in each case the level is independent of $\beta$ as long as $\beta\neq 0$ . The level also varies significantly with $\ell$ between these values. In light of this, one would reasonably conjecture that the smallest $\ell$ for which $U_{q,\ell}^{\beta}$ is in the $t$ -th level of the Clifford hierarchy is $\ell=2^{t}-1$ , for all sufficiently large finite fields of characteristic 2, and in each case the Clifford hierarchy level is independent of $\beta\neq 0$ . In general, a description of the diagonal Clifford hierarchy for prime-power dimensional qudits in terms of the degrees of the polynomials in the natural form (220) awaits further work.

## Abstract

In the setting of error-correcting codes with feedback, Alice wishes to communicate a $k$ -bit message $x$ to Bob by sending a sequence of bits over a channel while noiselessly receiving feedback from Bob. It has been long known (Berlekamp, 1964) that in this model, Bob can still correctly determine $x$ even if $\approx\frac{1}{3}$ of Alice’s bits are flipped adversarially. This improves upon the classical setting without feedback, where recovery is not possible for error fractions exceeding $\frac{1}{4}$ .

The original feedback setting assumes that after transmitting each bit, Alice knows (via feedback) what bit Bob received. In this work, our focus in on the limited feedback model, where Bob is only allowed to send a few bits at a small number of pre-designated points in the protocol. For any desired $\epsilon>0$ , we construct a coding scheme that tolerates a fraction $1/3-\epsilon$ of bit flips relying only on $O_{\epsilon}(\log k)$ bits of feedback from Bob sent in a fixed $O_{\epsilon}(1)$ number of rounds. We complement this with a matching lower bound showing that $\Omega(\log k)$ bits of feedback are necessary to recover from an error fraction exceeding $1/4$ (the threshold without any feedback), and for schemes resilient to a fraction $1/3-\epsilon$ of bit flips, the number of rounds must grow as $\epsilon\to 0$ .

We also study (and resolve) the question for the simpler model of erasures. We show that $O_{\epsilon}(\log k)$ bits of feedback spread over $O_{\epsilon}(1)$ rounds suffice to tolerate a fraction $(1-\epsilon)$ of erasures. Likewise, our $\Omega(\log k)$ lower bound applies for erasure fractions exceeding $1/2$ , and an increasing number of rounds are required as the erasure fraction approaches $1$ .
